“I stayed awake an extra hour watching” is a fact you can act on. “Porn has ruined everything” is too broad to guide the next evening.

items.t: A break from work I didn’t want to start
Less time to finish it

items: Give yourself a short, balanced account. “It distracted me from work I didn’t want to start. I then had less time to finish.” That sentence explains the appeal and the cost without asking you to deny either.
If the benefit was relief from a particular task, an alternative needs to address that task eventually. A walk can give you a break, but it won’t send the email.
If the benefit was sexual pleasure, an unrelated chore may not feel like an equivalent. You can still choose the chore or another activity because it serves something you value.

sections.title: Plan one difficult hour
items: Today, write the immediate benefit and one real cost beside each other. Save them for Day 32. Don’t make a dramatic list to frighten yourself into change. Include “unknown” where you lack information.
Use this account to plan one difficult hour in the next three days. Name the place, activity, and device rule, then set a check afterwards.
You’ll review what happened on Day 32. A clear picture of one evening is more useful than an argument about the whole of your life.

practice: Write an immediate benefit and a real cost of one recent or typical episode. Unknown is acceptable. Save them for Day 32.

Choose one likely difficult period in the next three days. Plan the place, activity, and device rule, with an accessible backup if plans change. Set a check after the period, by Day 32 where possible.
lessons.doneWhen: The notes, planned period, and review are saved. You’ll judge what helped after trying it.

lessons.title: Meet the need you can identify

openingQuote.text: We seek not to be free from pain, but to have something for which to bear pain.

closingQuote.text: The bait hides the hook.

sections.title: What you’d miss
items: An activity can be serving several purposes at once. Porn may offer arousal and also a way to stop thinking about work. Changing the viewing won’t necessarily finish the work or meet every other need.
Ask what you would miss if you stopped tonight. Be specific. Would you miss stimulation, privacy, a break, or the feeling of having something to look forward to?
There may be no single answer, and you don’t need to invent a deeper one.

sections.title: Choose what fits
items: Once you’ve named it, choose what fits. A break could be a short walk or music. Sexual desire raises the separate decisions discussed on Day 21.
Wanting company could lead to an invitation or a shared activity. If you’re avoiding work, give yourself a brief pause and then begin the first part.
Suppose you’re alone after dinner and want something enjoyable. Replacing browsing with a list of chores may make the evening feel like punishment.
A game, book, hobby, or conversation could be a better use of the time. The alternative should have a reason to exist beyond keeping you occupied.

sections.title: Try it briefly
items: Try one option for a short period today. You don’t have to keep it for the rest of the course. Notice whether it met the need you named and whether it helped you follow your porn rule. Those answers may differ.

If no option seems appealing, make the beginning easier or choose another time. It’s also reasonable to say that the exercise didn’t help. The notes should let you change the plan, not make you defend it.
Keep room for ordinary pleasure. Food, rest, friendship, and enjoyable activities aren’t prizes you earn by resisting an urge.
They belong in the day even when changing the habit is taking longer than you hoped.

question.prompt: What did you want from watching?
question.instr: Choose all that fit. Choose G alone if it fits.

opts.t: Sexual pleasure or arousal
A break from a task
Something interesting
Comfort or brief relief
A feeling of company or closeness
Something else
No recent example or no clear answer

fb.lead: Choose a response that fits the need and your boundary.
items: For sexual desire, check the Day 21 choice; another person isn’t a replacement available on demand. Unknown is fine.

practice: Name what you wanted from a recent urge and try a fitting response: rest, an interesting activity, appropriate contact, or a first step on a task.
For sexual desire, check or prepare the Day 21 boundary instead; sex or masturbation isn’t required. Record whether the response fit. If you don’t know the need, save a question for the next urge.
lessons.doneWhen: You’ve tried a response, prepared the sexual boundary, or saved an observation for later.

lessons.title: Begin a task you are avoiding

openingQuote.text: Until you make the unconscious conscious, it will direct your life and you will call it fate.

closingQuote.text: The unexamined life is not worth living.

sections.title: The visible problem
items: Sometimes the thing you’re avoiding is easy to name. The letter is unopened, the application unfinished, or the conversation postponed. Looking for a hidden reason can delay dealing with the visible one.
Ask whether there’s a problem you return to when browsing ends. If so, give it a first step.
You might read the letter, write the first sentence, book an appointment, or ask someone how to begin. Choose a step smaller than solving the entire problem.

sections.title: A clear next step
items: Masicampo and Baumeister ran experiments on unfinished goals and attention. Making specific plans could reduce some of the interference associated with unfinished tasks.
These laboratory findings don’t show that planning treats compulsive porn use. They do support testing whether a clear next step makes a nagging task easier to put down or begin.

items.t: “Deal with money.”
“Open the latest bill at six and write down the due date.”

items: For example, “Deal with money” leaves a large worry waiting. “Open the latest bill at six and write down the due date” gives you a place to start.
You may still need advice afterwards. The first step doesn’t have to include knowing the full answer.

If the problem needs another person, decide what request you can make. Write a short question in your own words. You can control making an appropriate enquiry; you can’t control an immediate response.

sections.title: When support comes first
items: Some situations need support before action, particularly when safety, abuse, or severe distress is involved.
Don’t turn “face the problem” into a requirement to confront someone or revisit a painful event alone. Choose a qualified service or safe contact when that fits.
Today, record the problem and first step, if there is one. Save it for Day 47.
If nothing clear comes to mind, leave the theory aside and keep the practical plan you’ve been using. An urge doesn’t require a secret explanation before you can close the screen.

practice: Ask whether an urge happened while you were avoiding something specific. If so, spend up to fifteen minutes on the smallest safe step, or request support if that needs to come first. Save a Day 47 follow-up.
If no avoided problem fits, use the Day 30 response or save a question for a future urge. Don’t search for a hidden issue to satisfy the exercise.
lessons.doneWhen: You’ve taken a first step or requested help, or prepared an alternative that fits.

lessons.title: Address one immediate cost

openingQuote.text: What is bought is cheaper than a gift.

closingQuote.text: Begin to live at once, and count each separate day as a separate life.

sections.title: One cost to address
items: Read the benefit and cost you recorded on Day 29. Then choose a cost you can address in the next day or two.
If watching delayed sleep, protect tonight’s bedtime. If it displaced work, begin the most necessary part. If it interrupted a meal, eat.
A list of everything you regret can become another hour spent thinking; one repair gives the day a beginning.

sections.title: Keep the cause specific
items: Keep the cause as specific as the evidence allows. “I watched instead of finishing the assignment” tells you what was delayed.
It doesn’t establish that every difficulty with study comes from porn. You may also need clearer instructions, more time, or help with the subject.
Suppose you stayed up late and now feel tired. Punishing yourself with an early alarm tomorrow could repeat the sleep problem.
A better repair may be ending browsing earlier tonight and allowing a realistic sleep period. The action should address the cost you named.

sections.title: A proportionate repair
items: Choose something proportionate. If a commitment was missed, make an honest apology or a new arrangement where appropriate.
If money or work has become a serious problem, seek relevant advice. You don’t have to resolve it before the lesson counts as read.
Use a short note: what happened, what needs attention, and when you’ll begin.
If there is no immediate repair, prepare for the next evening instead. You can keep the phone boundary or activity that’s already helping.

sections.title: Then let it rest
items: After taking the step, let the analysis end for now. Repeatedly reviewing the mistake doesn’t necessarily improve the repair. The meal, assignment, or conversation still deserves your attention.
When you check later, ask whether the action helped with the particular cost. Keep the answer honest.
It may have helped a little, revealed another obstacle, or shown you need more support. Each answer can guide a different next step.

practice: Review the period planned on Day 29: did it happen, did you follow the plan, and what needs changing? Keep the check for afterwards if the period is still ahead.
Read the benefit and cost you recorded. Choose one practical cost to address or prevent today. If the concern is mainly a values conflict, name it honestly and take a related action instead.
lessons.doneWhen: The review is recorded or rescheduled, and one fitting repair or preparation is made.

lessons.title: Make time for what viewing displaced

openingQuote.text: How we spend our days is, of course, how we spend our lives.

closingQuote.text: Great things are not done by impulse, but by a series of small things brought together.

sections.title: What was displaced
items: Repeated choices can affect things that matter over time: sleep, study, work, money, or relationships. To understand your own situation, look for what has actually been displaced.

Choose one area. What have you stopped doing, done less often, or found harder to keep? Use dates or examples if you have them. If the record is thin, say what you remember cautiously and begin observing now.
Avoid predictions about permanent damage or a future you’ve already lost. The course can’t tell you those things.
A missed month of a hobby is a reason to make time for it again. It isn’t proof that enjoyment will never return.

sections.title: A present decision
items: Suppose several evenings have gone to searching while you meant to practise music. The practical question is whether you can give music a place this week.
Put the instrument where you’ll use it and choose a short session. The long-term concern becomes a present decision you can try.
Relationships may need a different kind of action. If there’s an agreement about porn, understand what it says and discuss any breach honestly.
Choose an appropriate conversation rather than assume another person will welcome every detail or should become responsible for monitoring you.
Other factors may also be involved. Low mood, anxiety, conflict, or an unsuitable schedule can continue even when viewing changes.
If difficulties persist, ask for help with them instead of treating abstinence as the answer to everything.

sections.title: A little time today
items: Today, give one neglected person, responsibility, or activity a little time.
If it needs booking or another person’s availability, make the first arrangement. You can use an existing commitment rather than start a new project.

Later, notice whether you’ve begun giving that area more room. The useful comparison is between what you intended and what you did. A dramatic forecast is unnecessary when a small, real commitment is waiting.

practice: Choose an activity or commitment that viewing has displaced, if any. Give it a realistic block this week and begin a small part today, or make the needed invitation or booking.
If your main reason is a personal value rather than lost time, choose an action that follows it. Save what you chose and why. You don’t need a new improvement project.
lessons.doneWhen: You’ve begun a related action or made the arrangement and prepared what you can.

lessons.title: Make one change for tonight

openingQuote.text: The opportunity of defeating the enemy is provided by the enemy himself.

closingQuote.text: Victorious warriors win first and then go to war.

sections.title: The hour that goes wrong
items: Make one change that helps tonight. It doesn’t have to become a permanent system before you try it.
Choose the hour that most often goes wrong. What makes porn easy to begin there? The device beside you, an empty gap, or an activity you keep avoiding? Work on one of those details.
If the phone comes into bed, prepare another place for it while keeping necessary calls and alarms available.
If the gap after dinner is difficult, decide what you’ll do before dinner ends. If work is waiting, open the actual task and begin a small part before the feed.

sections.title: Close to the problem
items: Keep the action close to the problem. A better morning routine may be useful, but it won’t directly answer tonight’s habit of searching in bed.
The lesson is asking for a practical change at the point where you usually begin.

Try it once. If the difficult hour doesn’t occur today, practise the first steps and leave what you need ready. You won’t yet know how it works in that situation, and there’s no need to manufacture a test.

sections.title: After you try it
items: After actual use, ask what happened. Did you follow the change? Did you stop browsing when you intended?
Did something prevent you from starting the next activity? Record a sentence, then decide whether to repeat or adjust it.
Don’t dismiss a helpful change because it’s familiar. Moving the charger again isn’t progress if its current place already works. Use what’s helping and spend the time you saved on the day itself.
If the same change repeatedly fails, get more precise or add support. Perhaps you need an easier alternative, a clearer stopping point, or help with control that a device rule hasn’t addressed.
More severe promises won’t tell you which. The result of tonight’s attempt can help you choose.

practice: Choose the actual beginning of a recent difficult evening. Change one part you control and try the steps without opening porn.
If the setup already helped, keep it and name what made it practical. If no example is clear, prepare one observation for the next urge. Use the saved response when the situation occurs.
lessons.doneWhen: You’ve tried a change, confirmed a helpful setup, or prepared an observation. You don’t need another deletion when nothing remains.

lessons.title: Give an activity a place in the week

openingQuote.text: He who has a why to live can bear almost any how.

closingQuote.text: It is not length of life, but depth of life.

sections.title: A place in the week
items: A useful activity needs time in the week, not just a place on a list. Choose one you want to keep doing even on evenings without an urge.
It could be a class, a walk with someone, a hobby session, or another activity that fits your circumstances.
Reuse something already helping. Make the beginning manageable enough that attending doesn’t require an unusually energetic day.

sections.title: Four chances
items: Schedule four chances to do it. If another person is involved, make an invitation or check the booking.
You can begin arranging the activity without requiring someone else to accept immediately. Have a solo or accessible alternative where that would help.
Give each session a short check afterwards. We’ll also return to the plan on Days 42, 49, 56, and 63.
If the sessions happen later than those lessons, keep the checks for after they actually occur. A calendar date can’t tell you whether an activity helped before you’ve tried it.

sections.title: Your Day 21 choice
items: Also review the sexual boundary you chose on Day 21. Did it fit the change you wanted? Did it repeatedly lead to searching, or was it manageable?
Keep or adjust the rule from those observations. Masturbation remains a separate choice; there is no need to do it to complete this review.
If the record is unclear, keep the boundary simple and choose what to observe next.
You don’t need to force an answer about permanent abstinence today. Persistent loss of control or harm to daily life warrants qualified help.

sections.title: Take the first step
items: Take the first practical step towards the weekly activity: prepare materials, make a booking, or begin a short session. Then let it become part of life beyond the course.
The aim is to have something worth returning to, rather than spend every free evening checking whether you feel recovered.
The activity may be enjoyable, difficult, or a poor fit. The scheduled checks give you a chance to find out.

question.prompt: Looking back at the choice you made on Day 21, what fits?

opts.t: It fits my experience and values
One part needs changing
I want to end the temporary choice after reviewing it
I haven’t had a chance to assess it
I need qualified help with continuing difficulty or distress

fb.lead: Keep or change the separate masturbation choice from your experience, while keeping the porn rule clear.
items: If you haven’t had a chance to assess it, record that. Request help when needed.

practice: Review the choice from Day 21. Keep or adjust it from your experience; record unknown if you haven’t had a chance to assess it. Get help if ongoing control problems need it.
Choose one weekly activity and schedule four chances to do it. Prepare materials or make the first invitation or booking.
Set checks after the sessions. We’ll return on Days 42, 49, 56, and 63; keep later sessions’ checks for after they happen.
lessons.doneWhen: The boundary is reviewed, and the activity has dates, a first step, and review reminders.

lessons.title: Prepare a simpler response when tired

openingQuote.text: Energy and persistence conquer all things.

closingQuote.text: The art of being wise is the art of knowing what to overlook.

sections.title: No empty tank
items: An evening can be harder after poor sleep, stress, or a long shift. That doesn’t mean you have a fixed supply of willpower that has run empty.

The idea that self-control becomes depleted like fuel has been debated in research. A large, preregistered replication across 23 laboratories did not find convincing support for the predicted effect using its tested procedure.
That result doesn’t mean tiredness and stress have no effect. It means the simple empty-tank explanation isn’t secure enough to treat as a rule.

sections.title: A smaller version
items: Work with what you can observe. After a late shift, a complicated evening plan may be too much.
Put the phone away, eat something easy, and prepare for sleep. You can make the action smaller without deciding that further choice is impossible.
Prepare that smaller version ahead of time. If your usual hobby session takes an hour, decide what its first five minutes look like.
If cooking is too demanding, keep an easy meal available. If going outside isn’t possible, choose an indoor response.
You don’t have to turn a tired evening into a test. Close the content when you notice the search and use the simplest next action.
The urge may remain, but the whole plan doesn’t depend on winning a long argument with it.

sections.title: Remove a decision
items: Today’s question is practical: what can you remove from the decision?
A prepared meal, a visible reminder, or a book beside the chair can make the beginning easier. “Have more willpower” doesn’t specify a change.

Try the smaller version once, even if you’re feeling well. You’ll see whether anything is missing before you need it. After use on a difficult day, note whether it helped and what still needs attention.
If reduced expectations repeatedly leave serious problems untouched, seek more support. Keeping one night manageable is useful; it doesn’t replace help for ongoing loss of control or major distress.

question.prompt: You’ve had a demanding day. Which plan fits?

opts.t: Assume I can’t choose because my willpower is empty
Use a simple prepared response, with food or rest if needed
Do something exhausting to prove I’m committed

best.t: Use a simple prepared response, with food or rest if needed

items: Difficult circumstances matter, but self-control shouldn’t be treated as a fixed tank of fuel.

practice: Read your plan for a tired evening. Make one action simpler: an easy meal, a shorter activity, or a response you can begin indoors.
Prepare what it needs and try its first step without an urge. Save the smaller version under Bad day minimum. It should protect necessary care and fit the hour when you’ll use it.
lessons.doneWhen: The smaller response is ready and you’ve tried its beginning.

lessons.title: Practise the response

openingQuote.text: We are what we repeatedly do.

closingQuote.text: Excellence is an art won by training and habituation.

sections.title: Rehearse where it starts
items: Practise the response you want to remember. You don’t need an urge to check where the phone goes or how the next activity begins.
Choose one plan you’ve already written. Start where the habit normally starts: the chair, the bed, or the desk.
Close a harmless tab, move the device as planned, and begin the next action. This checks the steps in the place you’ll need them.
Notice the small obstacles. The book is elsewhere. The phone needs to remain available for calls. The activity is too noisy at night.
Change the plan so it fits. Repeating an instruction that can’t be followed won’t make it more practical.

sections.title: Keep it short
items: If you choose the urge-surfing exercise, practise the exercise itself: notice what is present, breathe normally for a brief pause, then begin the next activity.
Simply opening its page won’t show whether you know the steps. You don’t need to create a bodily sensation or urge.

Keep practice short. The purpose is to make the beginning familiar enough to try later, not spend the evening rehearsing every possible difficulty. One attempt and one adjustment are plenty for today.

sections.title: Practice and real use
items: When an urge next appears naturally, use the plan. Record whether it helped you stop and move on.
That is different information from checking whether the book and charger were ready. Preparation matters, but a comfortable rehearsal can’t establish the result during an urge.
There may be no opportunity today. Leave the steps ready and go on with another activity. Searching for triggering content would turn preparation into a different exercise with an unnecessary risk.
If the plan repeatedly fails at the same point, examine that point. Perhaps the first step is too late, the alternative doesn’t fit the hour, or you need more help.
Practice should make those details visible rather than hide them behind another promise.

practice: Practise one response from the place where you usually begin browsing. Close a harmless tab, put the device away, and begin the next action. If you choose an urge exercise, practise its steps and ending too.
Fix one awkward detail. Leave the steps ready for the next naturally occurring urge, and record that result later.
lessons.doneWhen: You’ve practised the response and saved an adjustment if needed. No urge or triggering material is required.

lessons.title: Keep rules that serve a purpose

openingQuote.text: No man is more unhappy than he who never faces adversity.

closingQuote.text: Nothing is so fatiguing as the eternal hanging on of an uncompleted task.

sections.title: Not the harshest rule
items: Discipline isn’t proved by choosing the harshest rule. A rule should help you do something useful and be clear enough to follow.
The marshmallow experiments are often told as a story about children with strong or weak willpower. Later work complicates that account.
Celeste Kidd and colleagues found, in a small experiment of 28 children, that an adult’s earlier reliability affected how long children waited.
Another study by Tyler Watts and colleagues found that associations between waiting and later outcomes became much smaller after accounting for background factors and earlier abilities.
Those findings aren’t lessons about porn treatment. They are a reason to be cautious about using one difficult choice as a verdict on someone’s character. Circumstances and expectations matter too.

sections.title: What is the rule for?
items: Look at your own rules. Does the rule protect sleep, time, or an agreement you value? Can you tell when you’ve kept it?
Does it still make sense on a difficult day? If its purpose is mainly to hurt or shame you, reconsider it.

items.t: Putting the phone away at bedtime
Missing meals after a slip

items: For example, putting the phone away at bedtime has a clear connection to late-night browsing.
Missing meals after a slip doesn’t. The latter removes something you need without addressing how the search began or ended.

sections.title: One useful rule
items: Choose one useful rule and write its reason. Keep its smallest workable version available for days with less time or energy.
Flexibility about the size of an activity can help you continue while keeping the porn boundary clear.
You may still dislike following the rule in the moment. That’s different from it being pointless. Judge it from its purpose and what happens when you use it.
Today, use or rehearse the rule once. If it has no clear benefit, change the detail or remove the optional demand. You don’t need to make the course harder to prove you take it seriously.

practice: Choose one rule you follow and write what it protects. If it’s useful, keep it and use or practise it once today.
If an optional rule mainly punishes you or has no clear purpose, change or remove that demand. Keep needed care. Discuss professional treatment changes with the relevant clinician.
lessons.doneWhen: You’ve kept or changed the rule for a clear reason and taken the fitting action.

lessons.title: Practise the part that gets in the way

openingQuote.text: Order and simplification are the first steps toward mastery.

closingQuote.text: Divide each difficulty into as many parts as is feasible and necessary to resolve it.

sections.title: Where you get stuck
items: Self-control involves several actions you can work on separately. You might need to notice earlier, begin a response sooner, or keep doing something else while the urge remains.

head: If you…
Work on
rows: Notice only after searching has begun
A first action that takes little thought
What you’ll do in the new room

items: Find the point that usually stops you. If you notice only after searching has begun, choose an earlier sign.
If you notice but keep bargaining, prepare a first action that takes little thought. If you move rooms and then reopen the content, work on what you’ll do in the new room.

These are different problems. Adding another reminder won’t help much when you already notice the cue but the next activity is missing. A longer explanation won’t prepare dinner or put the book within reach.

sections.title: Practise one part
items: Choose just one part today. For noticing, place a short reminder where the search normally begins. For beginning, practise putting the device away and standing up.
For continuing, give a suitable activity a few minutes while letting the feeling remain in the background.
Suppose you successfully put the phone on the shelf but keep returning to it because you have nothing else planned.
Prepare a short activity before the evening. You can still decide later whether you want a longer session. The first few minutes give you somewhere to begin.

Practise without deliberately provoking an urge. Check whether the action fits your space and circumstances. After you use it during an urge, record which part helped and which part remained difficult.

sections.title: What the attempt shows
items: Don’t ask the attempt to prove you’re a disciplined person. Ask whether you could recognise and follow a useful step. That gives you something to repeat or change.
If the problem is bigger than one missing step, add support. A qualified professional can help assess ongoing difficulty.
This lesson is a way to make a practical problem more specific; it isn’t a requirement to solve everything through repeated exercises alone.

question.prompt: Which part of the plan is hardest to follow?

opts.t: Getting started
Stopping
Remembering
Waiting with a feeling without acting straight away
Returning after an interruption
Another part, or no clear difficulty

fb.lead: Practise that part briefly without triggering material.
items: A reminder may help remembering; an easier beginning may help starting. Keep what works if no change is needed.

practice: Choose the part that gets in the way: noticing, remembering, beginning, stopping, continuing while tempted, or returning after interruption.

Try one small change for that part. Add a visible cue, shorten the beginning, prepare the next activity, or practise returning to it. Use harmless content and record what made the step easier or harder.
lessons.doneWhen: You’ve practised the useful part and recorded one result. If nothing needs changing, confirm what works.

lessons.title: Let a thought remain while you act

openingQuote.text: You don’t have to control your thoughts. You just have to stop letting them control you.

closingQuote.text: Men are disturbed not by things, but by the views which they take of things.

sections.title: A thought can stay
items: A thought can stay in your head while you choose another action. “One quick look” doesn’t have to become a search just because it has appeared.

Trying never to have a particular thought can make you watch for it constantly. In Daniel Wegner’s white-bear experiments, attempts to suppress a thought were followed by more of it in a later period.
This was a laboratory task, not a universal rule about every unwanted thought. It offers a reason to try something other than repeatedly demanding that the mind stop.

sections.title: Name it, then act
items: Name the thought briefly: “There’s the quick-look idea again.” Then begin the response you’ve chosen.
Close the content, move the device, and start what fits the hour. You don’t need a clever phrase, and you don’t need to repeat it until you feel different.
The same applies to feelings. Desire, boredom, or disappointment can be present while you make food or prepare for bed.
Letting a feeling remain doesn’t mean agreeing to act on every suggestion that comes with it.
If noticing the thought turns into more rumination, shorten the pause and move straight to a practical action.
This isn’t an instruction to spend the evening examining your mind. Use the amount of attention that helps you act.

sections.title: Try it today
items: Today, try the sentence with an ordinary distracting thought, if one appears. Then return to the task you were doing. Don’t deliberately summon sexual images to practise.
Later, notice whether the thought disappeared, returned, or stayed. Also notice what you did. Keeping your boundary while still feeling tempted is a possible outcome, not a contradiction.

If intrusive thoughts or distress are consuming a lot of your day, seek appropriate help. The course can offer a brief response, but persistent difficulties deserve more than a demand to think differently.

question.prompt: The thought is “one quick look.” What can you do next?

opts.t: Wait until the thought has completely disappeared
Notice the thought, close any content, and begin my response
Keep the content open while debating what to do

best.t: Notice the thought, close any content, and begin my response

items: A thought can remain while you choose another action.

practice: When an ordinary distracting thought appears, name it briefly and return to the task. You can use “There’s that thought again,” or your own words.
For a naturally occurring porn urge, close the content and begin the saved response without waiting for the thought to disappear. If no thought appears, read the steps once and leave them ready.
lessons.doneWhen: You’ve tried the response or prepared it for later. Don’t summon sexual thoughts for practice.

lessons.title: Give the action a time and place

openingQuote.text: Some things are in our control and others not.

closingQuote.text: Waste no more time arguing what a good man should be. Be one.

sections.title: When and where
items: Decide when and where the next action starts. “I’ll make time” leaves the decision waiting for later.
In a workplace vaccination study, employees prompted to write a date and time were more likely to get vaccinated than the control group.
The increase was about 4.2 percentage points above a control rate of 33.1 percent; a date-only prompt didn’t produce a statistically clear increase.
This was a vaccination intervention. It illustrates how a specific plan can help a task happen, without proving that planning works equally for every habit.

sections.title: Cue and first action
items: Use the idea for one decision you keep postponing. Write the cue, first action, and what you need ready.
“After dinner, I’ll put the phone on the shelf and read the book beside the chair” is easier to begin than “I’ll have a healthier evening.”
Choose a cue that actually happens in your day. If shift times vary, a regular event may be better than a fixed clock time.
If another person is needed, include the enquiry or invitation you can make now and another action while you wait.
Try the beginning once. Can you reach the materials? Is the place available? Does the first step still fit when you’re tired? Fix one problem rather than write a more ambitious plan.

sections.title: After you use it
items: You can use a commitment already in your notes. The course doesn’t require a new project every day. Repeating the same helpful action is often the point.

After actual use, record what happened. If you missed it, ask whether you forgot, lacked time, or avoided starting. Those answers suggest different changes: a reminder, a shorter action, or help with the task.
Then choose the next chance. A missed plan doesn’t need a punishment attached. It needs an honest result and a decision about what you’ll do when the cue returns.

question.prompt: Which plan gives you a clear beginning?

opts.t: When I feel bad, become stronger
When I open that account after work, close it, put the phone away, and begin the activity I prepared
When anything goes wrong, change my whole routine

best.t: When I open that account after work, close it, put the phone away, and begin the activity I prepared

items: It says what to notice and what to do first. Check that the activity is ready at that hour.

practice: Write one cue and action for a decision you keep postponing. Reuse an existing commitment if it fits. Name when it begins and prepare the materials.
Try the first step today. If the cue hasn’t happened, practise with harmless content and name the next expected chance. Note one obstacle and adjust it if needed.
lessons.doneWhen: The plan has a clear cue, ready materials, and a tried beginning.

lessons.title: Plan for a difficult day

openingQuote.text: Fall seven times, stand up eight.

closingQuote.text: Do what you can, with what you have, where you are.

sections.title: A smaller day
items: Prepare a smaller day before you need one. Illness, travel, poor sleep, or extra work can make the usual plan unrealistic.
Choose two or three actions that protect the most necessary things. They might be eating, keeping the phone out of bed, and preparing for sleep.
Include medication or care you already need as directed. The list should fit your circumstances, not copy somebody else’s ideal routine.
Keep the porn rule clear while shrinking optional tasks. You can do a shorter hobby session or skip extra tracking without turning the day into permission to keep watching.
If an urge happens, use the simplest response you’ve prepared.

sections.title: A deliberate adjustment

items.t: An hour of exercise and a lesson
Phone away, an easy meal, sleep

items: Suppose the normal plan includes an hour of exercise and a lesson. On a late shift, you could put the phone away, eat an easy meal, and sleep instead.
That’s a deliberate adjustment. There’s no reason to add exercise at midnight just to make the day look complete.
Review the latest activity scheduled on Day 35, if it has happened. Did you attend? Did it fit? Would a shorter session or a different time help?
If the session is still ahead, keep the check for afterwards rather than invent an answer today.

sections.title: Keep it where you’ll find it
items: Write the smaller plan in a few lines and put it where you’ll find it. Try one part now, or confirm that the materials are ready.
When a difficult day arrives, the plan should be easier to read than a full lesson.
After that day, return to the usual routine when it fits. You don’t owe extra work to make up for having less energy.

If difficult days have become a difficult period, seek more support and adjust the plan for that reality. A small minimum can help you get through today; it doesn’t need to carry every problem indefinitely.

practice: Review the latest Day 35 session if it has happened. Record attendance, how it fit, and any change. If still ahead, keep its check for afterwards.
Under Bad day minimum, keep two or three necessary actions for a difficult day. Include the simplest response to porn and care you need.
Try one part or check it’s ready. Shorten optional tasks rather than make them a debt.
lessons.doneWhen: The activity review is recorded or rescheduled, and the smaller day is ready.

lessons.title: Learn from a slip

openingQuote.text: There is more in us than we know.

closingQuote.text: While there’s life, there’s hope.

sections.title: Stop first, review later
items: After a slip, stop the episode before trying to explain it. Close the content and return to what the hour needs. Review it later, when you can look at a few facts without continuing the search.
Choose the moment where the evening changed. What happened before opening the content? Which warning sign did you notice?
What stopped you from using the response? You don’t need to reconstruct every minute or collect explicit details.

sections.title: What research suggests
items: Research on substance use gives one reason to examine responses after setbacks. A trial involving 286 people compared usual aftercare with therapist-led relapse prevention and mindfulness-based relapse prevention after treatment.
Outcomes differed across follow-ups, with benefits for some measures. These were structured treatment groups, not a test of a self-guided porn course.
The useful parallel is that a setback can lead to a review of the help and skills being used. It doesn’t prove the person is beyond help, and it doesn’t mean every addiction needs the same treatment.

sections.title: One obstacle, one change
items: Suppose you noticed the urge but the planned walk wasn’t possible because it was late and unsafe to go out. Add an indoor option.
If the response was available but you kept negotiating for another video, move the first action earlier. If neither change seems sufficient, consider professional support.
Keep the review short: the event, the obstacle, and one change. You can use a recent episode, but there’s no need to create one for this exercise.
If nothing has happened, check whether your current steps still fit.

sections.title: Use what you learn
items: Then do something with the information. Prepare the alternative, change the reminder, or make the enquiry. An explanation is useful when it changes the next attempt.
If the episodes remain frequent or seriously affect daily life, get qualified help. Reviewing the same evening repeatedly isn’t a reason to postpone a more useful level of support.

practice: Review a recent slip or close call, if available. Close the content first. Later, write what happened before it, the first sign you noticed, and the obstacle to using your response.
Make one practical change or take a support step. If no example exists, check that your current after-slip steps still fit. Don’t create a mistake for the review.
lessons.doneWhen: The review leads to a change, a confirmed plan, or a request for help.

lessons.title: Take care and make a repair

openingQuote.text: Experience is the name everyone gives to their mistakes.

closingQuote.text: Failure is instructive. The person who really thinks learns quite as much from his failures as from his successes.

sections.title: Responsibility without punishment
items: Taking responsibility after a mistake doesn’t require treating yourself badly. Food, sleep, and appropriate care are still needed.

Breines and Chen tested brief self-compassion exercises across four experiments. Some participants showed greater motivation to improve or make amends; in one experiment, they spent more time studying after a difficult test.
These were short experimental tasks. They don’t establish a treatment for porn use, but they challenge the assumption that kindness must prevent effort.

sections.title: Describe it plainly
items: Describe the event without the insult. “I watched after deciding not to, and I stayed up late.”
Then name the next useful action: end browsing, prepare for sleep, or deal with a missed commitment. The factual sentence already allows responsibility.
If an agreement was broken, consider a proportionate repair. An apology or honest conversation may be needed.
Make it relevant to the person affected, rather than a demand that they reassure you or hear every detail.
Punishment can add another problem. Skipping meals after a slip leaves you hungry. A punishing workout can postpone sleep.
Calling yourself worthless may make you avoid the very people or tasks that need attention.

sections.title: Care and repair
items: Today, choose one act of care and one repair if a repair is needed. If there hasn’t been a recent mistake, keep the steps ready and continue with normal care. You don’t have to invent guilt to use this lesson.
You may still feel ashamed after taking the action. Feeling better isn’t the condition for eating, washing, or resuming the day. Give those things their time while the feeling settles or remains.
If shame or self-hatred is severe or persistent, ask for qualified support. A brief exercise may help with the next decision, but ongoing distress deserves attention beyond a daily lesson.
You can seek that help while continuing to work on the behaviour you want to change.

question.prompt: Which actions take responsibility after a slip?

opts.t: Stop watching and meet necessary needs
Identify a real consequence and make a fitting repair or request for help
Withhold food or sleep because I’m disappointed
Call myself worthless until the mistake feels serious enough

best.t: Stop watching and meet necessary needs
Identify a real consequence and make a fitting repair or request for help

items: Address the event and any consequence while keeping necessary care.

practice: Describe a recent mistake factually, without an insult. Take one normal act of care and a proportionate repair if needed. That might be food and an appropriate apology, or sleep and a rescheduled task.
If there hasn’t been a mistake, keep ordinary care and prepare the steps for later. You don’t need to invent guilt or a confession.
lessons.doneWhen: You’ve taken care of a need and addressed a real consequence where there is one.

lessons.title: Adjust the plan for today

openingQuote.text: Wherever there is a human being, there is an opportunity for kindness.

closingQuote.text: Be tolerant with others and strict with yourself.

sections.title: Days that ask for less
items: Some days ask for less. You’re ill, work runs late, sleep was poor, or several problems arrive together. The plan should account for that.
Use the smaller day you prepared on Day 42. Keep the most necessary care and the simplest steps for stopping porn.
Shorten optional activities. If an exercise doesn’t fit, postpone it without turning it into a debt.
For example, a planned hour at the gym may become a short walk or rest. A full cooking session may become an easy meal.
A lesson may wait until tomorrow. The adjustment should fit the reason the day is difficult.

sections.title: Less, not nothing
items: Notice when “less” quietly becomes abandoning everything. You may not have time for a hobby, but putting the phone away at bedtime could still be possible.
Choose what remains within reach rather than ask whether the entire routine can be completed.
If an urge appears, begin with the first action you control. Close the content and move the device or yourself as planned.
You can decide about the rest of the evening afterwards. Keep an indoor or accessible option for times the usual response is unavailable.
Tell someone about a practical need if that would help: a delayed deadline, an appointment, or extra support. You don’t have to disclose sexual details to ask for a meal, company, or help with work.

sections.title: Adapt one commitment
items: Today, adapt one commitment to the day you actually have. Record the change briefly if it will help you use it again. Otherwise, take the action and leave the notes alone.
If rough days keep repeating, reconsider the weekly plan or seek support for what’s happening.
A routine built for unusually easy days won’t become realistic through more self-criticism. Keep the useful parts and change what the circumstances require.

practice: Adapt one commitment to today’s circumstances. Shorten an activity, use the easier meal, or postpone an optional lesson while keeping necessary care and the porn response.
Use the Bad day minimum if it fits. If the day is going well, confirm the version you’d use when needed and keep today’s helpful routine.
lessons.doneWhen: You’ve followed a fitting version of the day or prepared it for a future difficulty.

lessons.title: Get support during a difficult period

openingQuote.text: The sun is new each day.

closingQuote.text: Although the world is full of suffering, it is full also of the overcoming of it.

sections.title: Longer than a bad day
items: A difficult period can last longer than a bad day. Grief, illness, conflict, or sustained pressure may need a different plan and more support.
Rebecca’s smoking story, published by the CDC, describes returning to smoking during a divorce after seven months without it. Later, wanting to be there for her grandson mattered in another attempt.
Her account also includes care for depression and running. It is a personal story, not evidence that exercise cures depression or that smoking treatment should be copied here.
What it makes clear is the importance of the surrounding situation. A return to an old behaviour may happen while other difficulties are changing.
Those difficulties deserve attention as well as the behaviour itself.

sections.title: What has become harder
items: Ask what has become harder lately. Is sleep disrupted? Are you alone more often? Are responsibilities beyond the time or energy available? Choose one practical adjustment and one source of help if needed.
You might reduce optional course tasks, ask for help with a responsibility, or check a clinician’s availability.
Keep food, rest, and necessary care. If support is needed now, make the enquiry rather than only saving a contact for the end of the course.
Use your smaller plan for a while and give it a review date. The purpose is to see whether it fits this period, not to promise you’ll feel normal by that date. If things worsen, review sooner.

sections.title: Asking for help
items: Personal contact may help, but another person’s immediate reply isn’t required to complete the step. Services can be the first choice and the backup when trusted contacts aren’t available.
Today, prepare what you’ll do during the next difficult evening and how you’ll ask for help.
You can continue working on porn use without expecting one brief exercise to carry every problem that has arrived with it.

question.prompt: What currently calls for a temporary change to the plan?
question.instr: Choose all that fit. Choose G alone if it fits.

opts.t: Illness or persistent symptoms
Grief, a breakup, or another major event
Exams or sustained work pressure
Moving, travel, or a changed schedule
Isolation or a change in contact
Something else
No difficult period right now

fb.lead: Choose an adjustment or support that fits.
items: If no difficult period applies, confirm your support details and keep the routine that works.

practice: If a difficult period is affecting the plan, choose one temporary adjustment and one support option.
Check how to access the help and make the enquiry if it’s needed now. Set a realistic date to review the adjustment.
If no difficult period fits, confirm the existing support details and leave the routine alone.
lessons.doneWhen: The fitting adjustment and support step are made, or the existing support is confirmed. A reply isn’t required.

lessons.title: Return to the task you postponed

openingQuote.text: Sometimes even to live is an act of courage.

closingQuote.text: The oak fought the wind and was broken, the willow bent when it must and survived.

sections.title: Back to Day 31
items: Look back at the problem you named on Day 31. Has the first step happened? If not, what made it hard to begin?
Sometimes the step was still too large. “Finish the application” may need to become “open it and find the deadline.”
Sometimes you lacked information or needed another person. Make the specific enquiry rather than keep rewriting the same intention.
A break can be useful, but give it an ending. You might walk for ten minutes and then read the letter.
If the break keeps expanding into another lost evening, prepare the first step before taking it and choose when you’ll return.

sections.title: A first sentence
items: Suppose an unanswered email keeps bothering you. You don’t yet know what to say, so you keep opening videos. Begin by writing the question you need answered, or a rough first sentence.
The task may still take time, but you’ve stopped asking yourself to produce the whole finished answer before starting.
Not every problem should be faced alone. A harmful relationship, unsafe workplace, or upsetting memory may require support before action.
This exercise doesn’t require confrontation, disclosure, or writing about a painful event. A safer first step can be contacting an appropriate service.

sections.title: One step today
items: If the Day 31 problem has been resolved, leave it resolved. Choose a current small task only if one is genuinely waiting. If no avoidance problem fits, use the time for an activity you value instead.
Today, take one step on the actual issue. Make it clear enough that you’ll know whether it happened. Save any further step with a realistic time, then let the rest of the day continue.
Dealing with a task may reduce a worry or may simply get the task moving. Either can be useful.
It doesn’t need to remove an urge to justify the effort, and an urge doesn’t need a hidden cause before you can stop watching.

practice: Return to the Day 31 first step. If it hasn’t happened, make it smaller or request the information or help you need. Spend up to fifteen minutes on the safe step now.
If the issue is resolved, choose another small waiting task only if one exists. If none fits, keep a valued activity. Get support before action when safety or severe distress is involved.
lessons.doneWhen: You’ve taken a fitting action or made the support request. Confrontation or painful reflection isn’t required.

lessons.title: Begin the next part of the day

openingQuote.text: The cave you fear to enter holds the treasure you seek.

closingQuote.text: Nothing diminishes anxiety faster than action.

sections.title: The next necessary thing
items: The day still contains the hours that remain. A slip, a late start, or a missed task doesn’t decide what happens next.
Look at the clock and choose the next necessary thing. Late at night, that may be washing and bed.
In the afternoon, it may be lunch, an appointment, or a small piece of work. The answer should fit the hour rather than an attempt to make the record look perfect.
Use the steps you’ve already written after a slip. Close the content first. Don’t keep browsing while planning a better tomorrow. If the steps no longer fit, change one detail and begin.

sections.title: Smaller is fine
items: Suppose you lost an hour you wanted for study. Trying to recover it by studying deep into the night may create another cost.
You could do the most necessary ten minutes, plan the next session, and keep bedtime. The lost hour remains lost, but it doesn’t have to take tomorrow’s morning too.
Choose a smaller action when needed. Send the enquiry instead of solving the whole problem.
Prepare materials instead of completing the full session. Eat something easy instead of turning dinner into another demanding task.

sections.title: Back to the day
items: If the day has been going well, keep a useful commitment. There is no need to revisit every possible mistake just because the lesson concerns recovery after one. A planned activity or normal care is enough.
After taking the step, stop checking whether you’ve rescued the day. Give the meal, conversation, or rest your attention. Returning to life is easier when you let the next activity have its time.
Today’s practice is one concrete return. You don’t need to feel proud, forgiven, or fully motivated before beginning.
If serious difficulty remains, add a request for help. That can also be a practical use of the hour you still have.

practice: Look at the hour and choose the next necessary activity: food, work, class, washing, or bed. After a slip, close the content and follow your saved steps first.
Begin a manageable part. If the day is going well, keep a useful existing commitment instead. Don’t add punishment to compensate for lost time.
lessons.doneWhen: You’ve returned to one activity that fits the hour.

lessons.title: Take a step after a longer setback

openingQuote.text: Begin anywhere.

closingQuote.text: The beginning is always today.

sections.title: After a longer setback
items: A longer setback can make the future feel smaller. You may think the lost weeks or months have decided what’s possible now. Start with a decision that can still be made.
Choose one area that needs attention: work, study, health, money, or a relationship. What is the next action, and who can help with it? A first enquiry is often enough for today.
If work has fallen behind, ask about the necessary next task or deadline. If money is causing difficulty, check an appropriate advice service.
If control over porn use remains poor and life is seriously affected, seek qualified assessment. The course doesn’t need to be finished first.

sections.title: A useful beginning
items: Don’t promise a dramatic comeback. A useful beginning may be an appointment, a reopened assignment, or an invitation. Its size doesn’t tell you how serious the problem is. It tells you what can be done now.
Review the latest activity from Day 35 if it has occurred. Did you attend, and did it deserve the time?
If circumstances interrupted it, decide whether a shorter session or another date fits. If it’s still ahead, keep the check for afterwards.
You can maintain something already working while addressing the larger difficulty.
A meal, sleep routine, or trusted contact may remain useful even when the overall record is disappointing. Keep the value of those actions separate from the need for more help.

sections.title: Begin from here
items: Today, take one step and write the next only if it’s needed. If waiting for another person, choose something you can do while waiting rather than repeatedly checking for a reply.
The past may have real consequences. You don’t need to deny them to begin again. Work from the situation as it is, with whatever care, advice, or treatment it now requires.
That gives the next week a specific beginning instead of another verdict about your life.

practice: Review the latest Day 35 session if it’s happened; keep the check for afterwards if not.
Confirm your support details. If control or daily life is seriously affected, check a qualified professional’s availability or request an appointment.
If another area needs advice, make the fitting enquiry. You can use a service when no safe personal contact is available.
lessons.doneWhen: The activity review is recorded or rescheduled, and support details are checked or a needed request is made.

lessons.title: Give an activity time before switching

openingQuote.text: The gods were bored; therefore they created human beings.

closingQuote.text: Boredom is the root of all evil, the despairing refusal to be oneself.

sections.title: Jumping between clips
items: Boredom can send you searching for something more interesting, then keep you switching when nothing feels interesting enough. More choice doesn’t always improve the experience.

Katy Tam and Michael Inzlicht tested switching between or within videos across seven experiments involving 1,223 participants. Switching could increase boredom compared with watching without switching.
Results involving articles and some samples were less conclusive. The finding concerns those tested media tasks; it doesn’t show that every screen activity causes boredom.
Think about an evening spent jumping between clips. Each switch promises a better one.
You finish without having enjoyed much or given another activity time to become interesting. If that pattern fits, try changing the switching rather than searching harder.

sections.title: Give one activity time
items: Choose one activity for a short period. Reading, a game, music, a hobby, movement, or rest can all fit.
Give it enough time to begin before opening unrelated feeds. A device is fine when it’s part of the activity or needed for accessibility.
You may feel bored at first. Notice whether that changes once you’ve started. If it stays dull, the activity may be a poor fit, or you may need rest or company.
You aren’t required to call boredom good or enjoy a task because you chose it.

sections.title: What the result tells you
items: Use the result to decide what to keep. “Ten minutes of drawing held my attention” suggests something different from “I was too tired and wanted sleep.” Both are more useful than “I need more stimulation.”
Today, try one suitable activity without unrelated switching, then record a sentence about how it went. Don’t make the exercise another demand to avoid every screen.

If boredom is persistent alongside low mood or loss of interest in much of life, seek appropriate help. A lesson about switching is a narrow tool, and it doesn’t explain every reason an evening feels empty.

question.prompt: What did the video-switching experiments find?

opts.t: Every screen activity increases boredom
Switching increased boredom in some of the video tasks tested
Everyone needs to avoid entertainment

best.t: Switching increased boredom in some of the video tasks tested

items: Results were less conclusive for other formats and some samples. Try a change only where the switching is a problem for you.

practice: Try ten to fifteen minutes of one activity without unrelated switching. Choose reading, a hobby, work, movement, or rest according to what you need. Devices are fine when they serve the activity.
Record whether it became easier to enter, stayed dull, or didn’t fit. Choose one adjustment if useful.
lessons.doneWhen: You’ve tried the activity and noted what happened. Enjoyment isn’t required.

lessons.title: Choose what begins in an empty gap

openingQuote.text: Nothing is more intolerable to man than a state of complete repose.

closingQuote.text: All of humanity’s problems stem from man’s inability to sit quietly in a room alone.

sections.title: The transition
items: The quickest activity to begin often wins the empty gap. The phone is in your hand before you’ve decided what you want from the break.
Look for the transition. Did you open a harmless feed and then start searching sexually? Did work end with no plan for the next hour?
If a particular account or search repeatedly begins the behaviour you want to stop, include it in the boundary.

sections.title: A specific rule
items: Keep the rule specific. “After dinner, I’ll begin the book before opening unrelated feeds” is something you can try.
“Use screens less” leaves you deciding what less means every evening. Necessary calls, work, and accessibility still need to fit.
Prepare a different beginning. Put the activity within reach, choose a short first part, and name when the break ends.
You don’t have to build a full evening schedule. One ready action can change what happens in a ten-minute gap.
Suppose you usually open a feed while waiting for food. You could keep music or a book ready for that time.
If the screen habit isn’t causing difficulty, leave it alone and work on the situation that actually matters. The course isn’t asking you to manufacture a problem with every form of leisure.

sections.title: Try it in a normal gap
items: Try the change during a normal gap today. If that gap doesn’t happen, prepare it for the next one. Don’t reopen triggering content to see whether you can resist.
Afterwards, ask whether the alternative was easy to begin and whether it helped you keep the boundary. If you returned to the search, look at the first point where the change stopped helping.
The useful result is a clearer beginning and ending. You can keep a harmless feed when it fits your life and change the particular habit that keeps leading somewhere you didn’t intend to go.

practice: If a feed or unplanned gap often leads to porn, write a specific stopping rule or alternative. Keep it under Access or First response.
During a normal gap today, begin the alternative before opening the usual feed and try it for ten minutes.
If the pattern doesn’t fit, leave normal screen use alone and note the actual problem to work on instead.
lessons.doneWhen: You’ve tried a fitting change or recorded that this pattern doesn’t apply. No risky browsing is needed.

lessons.title: Try fifteen minutes without switching

openingQuote.text: Seek not that the things which happen should happen as you wish; but wish the things which happen to be as they are.

closingQuote.text: Patience is bitter, but its fruit is sweet.

sections.title: Fifteen minutes
items: Give one slower activity a little time before deciding it isn’t enough. Some things become interesting after you’ve begun rather than in the first few seconds.
Choose fifteen minutes of reading, a hobby, a task, gentle movement, or rest. Keep unrelated feeds closed while you try it.
You can use a device when it’s part of the activity; the point is to give the activity your attention.
Suppose you begin a book and reach for a new clip after the first paragraph. Put the phone aside and read a little further before changing.
You may still decide the book isn’t for you. The difference is that you’ve given it a chance instead of comparing its opening seconds with a constantly changing feed.

sections.title: Not an endurance test
items: Don’t turn this into sitting still through discomfort for its own sake. If you’re exhausted, rest may be the better choice.
If the activity is inaccessible or unpleasant, adjust it. Boredom isn’t an achievement to collect.

At the end, ask what happened. Did the activity become easier to enter? Did it remain dull? Did you need a different kind of break? Keep the answer short and specific enough to choose what to do next.
If it helped, leave the materials ready for another session. If it didn’t, choose another option later. You don’t need to defend the first choice or force a daily habit from one attempt.

sections.title: A clear ending
items: This practice may also show how frequently you switch without thinking. You can notice a reach for the phone and return to the page without treating the reach itself as a failure.
Today, let the fifteen minutes have a clear ending. Move on to the next thing afterwards.
The exercise is a short chance to see how an activity feels when it receives attention, not a rule that every free hour must be slow, quiet, or screen-free.

practice: Give one activity fifteen minutes without unrelated switching. Choose what fits: reading, a hobby, a task, gentle movement, or rest. Keep needed devices in use and unrelated feeds closed.
At the end, record whether it became easier to enter, stayed dull, or wasn’t right for the moment. Then begin the next part of the day.
lessons.doneWhen: You’ve tried the activity and recorded its fit. It needn’t be enjoyable or screen-free.

lessons.title: Change one screen habit

openingQuote.text: The things you own end up owning you.

closingQuote.text: The price of anything is the amount of life you exchange for it.

sections.title: The habit causing trouble
items: Choose the screen habit that is actually causing trouble. Screens can support work, reading, friendship, and accessibility as well as make unwanted browsing easy.
In a small laboratory study, Anne-Marie Chang and colleagues compared prolonged evening reading on a light-emitting device with print.

The device condition affected sleep-related measures, including sleep timing. Those controlled exposures weren’t a brief phone check, so the study doesn’t justify treating every screen use as equally harmful.

For this course, begin with what you’ve observed. Is the phone in bed keeping you awake or making porn easy to reach? Is a particular feed repeatedly leading to searches? Change that use, place, or time.

sections.title: State the rule
items: State the rule plainly: no unrelated feeds in bed, or put the laptop away after finishing the specified work.
Keep necessary calls, alarms, care, and accessibility available. A rule that ignores those needs is likely to break for a good reason.
Use an existing rule if it’s helping. There is no need to add another boundary just to make this week’s lesson different. You can check whether the current setup still fits.
Prepare the device or room and follow the rule once when the situation occurs. If it doesn’t happen today, name when you’ll first try it. Set a Day 60 reminder to review the week.

sections.title: Review it on Day 60
items: At that review, ask whether you followed the rule, whether it helped, and what got in the way. A reduction in one feed that leaves you awake on another may need a different change. Keep mixed results mixed.
The aim is to make the troublesome part easier to manage while keeping the device useful. You don’t need to declare all screens bad before putting one of them away for the evening you want to have.

question.prompt: Which screen habit will you try changing this week?

opts.t: Browsing in bed
Using the device where I usually start watching porn
Continuing to browse after work on the device ends
Another particular habit or time
I’ll keep an existing rule that helps
No clear screen habit needs changing

fb.lead: Name the use, place, or time, while keeping essential functions.
items: Review what happens on Day 60. You can keep a helpful rule instead of adding another.

practice: Choose one screen rule for the problem you’ve observed. Name the use, time, or place it covers, while preserving necessary calls, alarms, work, care, and accessibility.
Prepare the setup and follow the rule when the situation happens. Otherwise name the first expected chance. Reuse an existing helpful rule if it fits, and set a Day 60 review.
lessons.doneWhen: The rule and setup are ready, with first use completed or planned and the review saved.

lessons.title: Try an hour away from one feed

openingQuote.text: Abstinence is easier than perfect moderation.

closingQuote.text: Simplicity is the ultimate sophistication.
closingQuote.by: Commonly attributed to Leonardo da Vinci

sections.title: What an hour can show
items: A “dopamine detox” doesn’t remove dopamine from the brain, and this course can’t promise to reset a reward system by taking away screens. Dopamine has several roles in learning and motivation.
You can still try a simpler, useful experiment: set aside one automatic feed or browsing habit for an hour and see when you reach for it.
Choose a habit that’s causing difficulty, rather than remove every enjoyable activity.
Keep necessary calls, work, care, and accessibility available. The porn boundary you chose stays in place for the whole day; this hour is about an additional habit you want to understand.

sections.title: Notice the reach
items: Notice the reach and what was happening. Were you waiting, avoiding a task, wanting company, or looking for a break? You might not know. Write “unsure” if so, then choose something suitable for the time.
Suppose you check the same feed every time a task becomes difficult. Closing the feed doesn’t make the task easier.
You may need to find the confusing instruction, ask a question, or take a short break with an ending. The hour can make that pattern easier to see.

sections.title: At the end of the hour
items: At the end, decide whether a small rule would help. Maybe the feed stays closed during the first ten minutes of work.
Maybe the existing bedtime rule is enough. If the habit isn’t causing a problem, leave it alone and review a change that’s relevant.
You may feel restless, calmer, or much the same. None of those feelings measures a brain reset. Judge the experiment from what you did and what you learned about the habit.
Today, keep the observation brief.
The purpose is to make a decision about a particular use of time, not create another system for monitoring every pleasure or repeatedly checking whether you’re recovering correctly.

question.prompt: What can an hour away from one feed tell you?

opts.t: That dopamine has been removed from my brain
When I wanted to check the feed and what I did instead
That my porn boundary ends when the hour ends

best.t: When I wanted to check the feed and what I did instead

items: You’re observing one habit. Your porn boundary continues after the hour.

practice: Set aside one troublesome automatic feed or browsing habit for an hour. Keep essential functions and your porn boundary in place.
Notice when you reach for the habit and what you wanted then. At the end, decide whether a small lasting rule would help. If no such habit is causing trouble, review an existing useful rule instead.
lessons.doneWhen: The hour and observation are complete, or you’ve reviewed the rule that fits your situation.

lessons.title: Prepare the first hour after waking

openingQuote.text: Lose an hour in the morning, and you will spend all day looking for it.

closingQuote.text: The secret of your future is hidden in your daily routine.

sections.title: Decide the night before
items: If the first hour after waking is difficult, decide its first activity before you go to bed. You shouldn’t have to invent the morning while already scrolling.
Choose what fits: washing, breakfast, a short piece of work, a walk, or another necessary activity.
Prepare the materials. Set a realistic alarm that allows enough rest rather than use an early start as punishment.
Marcus Aurelius wrote about getting up to do the work of a human being.
You can take that as a prompt to begin a chosen responsibility, without borrowing an emperor’s schedule or making productivity the purpose of every morning.

sections.title: Fit your real schedule
items: Suppose you usually wake, open a feed, and search before getting out of bed.
Put the phone where you can keep needed alarm or call functions, and decide where you’ll go first. Breakfast already partly prepared can give you an easier beginning.
If you work nights, apply the idea to your waking period rather than a conventional morning.
If you’re ill or caring for someone, rest or care may be the first thing the day needs. The routine should serve the real schedule.
There may be no morning problem. Confirm what’s working and leave it alone. You don’t need to change every part of life because the course has a lesson about it.

sections.title: Check how it goes
items: Save a short check for the next time you wake. Did you begin the chosen activity? Was anything missing?
We’ll revisit that result tomorrow if the morning has happened; otherwise keep the reminder for afterwards.
Today, prepare one beginning or keep the routine that’s already useful. A morning plan doesn’t need many steps.
It needs something you can start, the materials to start it, and room for the amount of rest your circumstances require.

practice: If the hour after waking is difficult, choose its first activity and prepare the materials. Set an alarm that allows enough rest. Keep needed phone functions and decide when unrelated feeds can begin.
If the waking routine already works, confirm it. Save a short check for after the next waking period; we’ll revisit it on Day 56 if it has happened.
lessons.doneWhen: The first activity and check are ready, or you’ve confirmed the routine that’s helping.

lessons.title: Give time to something that matters

openingQuote.text: He who has a why to live can bear almost any how.

closingQuote.text: Life can only be understood backwards; but it must be lived forwards.

sections.title: Time for what matters
items: What deserves some of the time you’re trying to recover? Choose a person, activity, or responsibility with a reason that makes sense to you.
Meaning needn’t arrive as a feeling before you begin.
You can spend time with someone because the relationship matters, practise a skill because you want to learn it, or rest because your health needs it. The first session may feel ordinary.

Seneca’s first letter asks the reader to take care of time. For today’s lesson, make that practical: give something you value a place in the day, rather than spend the whole evening thinking about wasted hours.

sections.title: Make the time
items: Choose fifteen to thirty minutes, or a smaller block when needed. If another person or booking is involved, make the invitation or arrangement.
You can reuse the weekly activity from Day 35 instead of starting a project.
First review the latest Day 35 session and the waking routine from yesterday, if each has occurred. What did you try, and what happened?
If either is still ahead, keep its check for afterwards. If the routine didn’t fit, change one detail.
Then begin the chosen activity. Put the materials within reach, make the call, or open the first part of the task.
Give it attention for the time available. It doesn’t have to produce a dramatic sense of purpose.

sections.title: Enough as it is
items: When low mood or loss of interest is persistent, appropriate support may be needed.
A valued activity can be part of care without becoming a promised cure. Keep professional help available when the problem extends beyond an empty evening.
Today, record the action if it helps you plan another session. Otherwise, let the action be enough.
The point of making time is to use it, not turn every enjoyable or meaningful moment into another recovery measurement.

practice: Review the latest Day 35 session and yesterday’s waking plan if they have happened. Record what you tried and any adjustment. Keep future checks for afterwards.
Name one person, responsibility, or activity that matters to you and give it fifteen to thirty minutes, or make the needed invitation or booking. You can reuse an existing activity.
lessons.doneWhen: The reviews are recorded or rescheduled, and you’ve taken the chosen action or made its arrangement.

lessons.title: Arrange a shared activity

openingQuote.text: What do we live for, if it is not to make life less difficult for each other?

closingQuote.text: The greatest thing in the world is to know how to belong to oneself.

sections.title: Actual time
items: Give a relationship some actual time. Thinking that you should connect more won’t arrange a conversation or put a shared activity in the week.
The Harvard Study of Adult Development is often cited for the association between relationships and wellbeing.

Its long-term observations are valuable, but they don’t show that one invitation will cause better health or make porn use easy to change. Use the finding as a reason to pay attention to relationships, with realistic expectations.

sections.title: A specific invitation
items: Choose a person you trust or enjoy and suggest something specific: a walk on Saturday, a meal after work, or a call at a time that suits both of you.
Give them room to decline or suggest another time. Their answer isn’t a grade for the exercise.
If no safe personal contact is available, look for a regular class, group, community setting, or appropriate service you can access.
Check the time, cost, location, and how to attend. A concrete enquiry is a useful beginning.
You don’t need to disclose porn use to take part in ordinary contact. You can enjoy a meal or talk about a shared interest.
If you do want support with the problem, choose someone willing and appropriate, and explain what help you’re asking for.

sections.title: While you wait
items: Suppose an invitation gets no immediate reply. Send it once, then continue the evening.
Repeated checking doesn’t give the other person more time, and it can make the wait take over. Prepare another activity while the answer is unknown.
If your social life is already working, keep an existing plan and give it your attention. There’s no need to add contacts for the sake of completing a lesson.

Today, make the invitation, check attendance, or keep the shared activity. Save the details only where they’ll help you follow through. The relationship deserves time beyond its possible usefulness to recovery.

practice: Suggest an activity, day, and approximate time to someone you trust or enjoy. If no safe personal contact is available, check how to attend a regular group or access an appropriate service.
If social life is already working, keep a shared activity. Save details under Support or Weekly life only if they’ll help later.
lessons.doneWhen: The invitation or enquiry is made, or you’ve kept the shared activity. A reply isn’t required.

lessons.title: Choose contact that fits

openingQuote.text: We are all so much together, but we are all dying of loneliness.

closingQuote.text: Friendship is unnecessary, like philosophy, like art. It has no survival value; rather it is one of those things which give value to survival.

sections.title: Different kinds of loneliness
items: Loneliness can mean different things. You may have little contact, plenty of contact without closeness, or be missing one particular person. Choose a step that fits what you’re missing.
Sandstrom and Dunn studied everyday interactions with acquaintances as well as close ties.

Their findings linked more weak-tie interactions with greater wellbeing, but the observations don’t establish that brief contact cures loneliness. A familiar face can be worth greeting without carrying that much responsibility.

sections.title: A step that fits

head: If you…
Try
