rows: Know people, but feel close to no one
A one-to-one conversation with a safe person
Contact with people who are available

items: If you rarely see people, a regular shared activity may be a useful start. Seeing the same people again gives contact another chance to develop.
Check a group you can actually attend rather than make an ambitious list of possibilities.
If you know many people but don’t feel close to anyone, consider a one-to-one conversation with a safe person.
Share something modest and true, within your comfort. You don’t have to begin with the most private part of your life.
If you’re missing someone unavailable, seek contact or support from people who are available.
Another person can’t always give the reassurance you want, and repeated requests may cross a boundary. Grief and loss may also deserve qualified help.

sections.title: One action
items: There may be no loneliness problem today. Give a valued relationship some attention or keep a plan you’ve already made. The course doesn’t require you to reinterpret all solitary time as loneliness.
Choose one action: attend, invite, enquire, or make an appropriate call. You can control taking the step, not another person’s response or how quickly the feeling changes.
Afterwards, notice whether the type of contact fit. An enjoyable conversation doesn’t have to solve the whole problem to matter.
If the need remains, plan another reasonable step or seek support rather than call the first attempt a failure.

question.prompt: What kind of contact feels missing, if any?
question.instr: Choose all that fit. Choose G or H alone if it fits.

opts.t: Everyday company
A closer one-to-one conversation
A regular group or activity with the same people
Professional help with something difficult
I’m missing a particular person
Something else
No contact feels missing
I’m unsure

fb.lead: Choose a step that fits the answer.
items: If nothing is missing or you’re unsure, keep a valued interaction without forcing a new need.

practice: Choose the step that fits: more everyday contact through a shared activity, a one-to-one conversation with a safe person, or support from someone available when you’re missing a particular person.
Make an invitation, attend, or check a group or service. If you aren’t lonely, give a valued relationship some attention. Respect other people’s limits.
lessons.doneWhen: You’ve taken the chosen step. A reply or immediate change in loneliness isn’t required.

lessons.title: Choose how to spend time alone

openingQuote.text: All of humanity’s problems stem from man’s inability to sit quietly in a room alone.

closingQuote.text: Whosoever is delighted in solitude is either a wild beast or a god.

sections.title: Time alone, chosen
items: Time alone can be restful, enjoyable, or difficult. What you choose to do with it, and whether you have other contact available, can make a difference.
Choose a short period alone deliberately instead of letting an empty gap become unplanned browsing.
Read, make something, listen to music, walk, or rest. Use a device when it’s part of the activity, with unrelated feeds closed.
Name what follows. After twenty minutes of reading, you might prepare dinner. After a quiet break, return to work or a shared activity.
A clear ending can keep a chosen pause from turning into hours you didn’t intend to lose.

sections.title: Change the setting
items: If being alone tends to make urges harder, choose a shared place where you can still do your own activity: a library, café, or common room if accessible.
You don’t need to speak with anyone for the change of setting to be useful.
Suppose you enjoy drawing but usually start it in bed with the phone nearby. Move the materials to the table and put the phone elsewhere.
You’re making room for the activity you chose, rather than relying on a promise to ignore a device within reach.

sections.title: Try it briefly
items: Try ten to twenty minutes today and notice how it went. Was it restful, absorbing, uncomfortable, or a poor fit? Record one adjustment if needed. Don’t require the time to make you calm.

If solitude brings distress that feels unmanageable, stop and choose contact or appropriate support. This is a short leisure exercise, not exposure therapy or a test of how much isolation you can tolerate.
When the time ends, begin what you named next. Keeping the ending is part of the practice.
You can learn what kind of time alone suits you without making loneliness or total screen avoidance the price of completing it.

practice: Choose ten to twenty minutes for an activity alone, or a personal activity in a shared place. Decide what you’ll do and what follows it. Use necessary devices with unrelated feeds closed.
Try it and note whether it was restful, difficult, or unhelpful. Make one adjustment if needed. Stop and choose contact or support if it becomes too distressing.
lessons.doneWhen: You’ve tried a fitting activity and recorded the result, or stopped and chosen support.

lessons.title: Separate desire from wanting company

openingQuote.text: There is no instinct like that of the heart.

closingQuote.text: The hunger for love is much more difficult to remove than the hunger for bread.

sections.title: Desire or company?
items: Porn can offer an image of connection without providing the conversation, care, or mutual interest you may be wanting.
It can also be about sexual desire without a missing relationship behind it. Check your own situation rather than assume a single explanation.
If you want company, choose contact that fits: focused time with a willing partner or friend, an invitation, or a regular group.
If sexual desire is the main issue, look at the boundary from Day 21. You don’t need to do anything sexual to complete the lesson.

sections.title: Other people’s choices
items: Keep other people’s choices clear. A partner isn’t responsible for preventing an urge or available whenever you feel one.
Intimacy needs mutual interest and consent. A personal rule about porn can still be followed when someone else isn’t interested or nearby.
If there’s an agreement about viewing, make sure you understand it and can discuss it honestly. Don’t expect mind-reading, and don’t use the course as a reason to demand monitoring or reassurance.

sections.title: The screen review
items: Today also brings the Day 53 screen review. Did you follow the rule? Did it help with the particular problem? What was difficult?
Keep, adjust, or end that additional screen experiment from what happened. Ending an unhelpful screen experiment doesn’t automatically change your porn boundary.
If you haven’t had a chance to use the rule, keep the check for after you do. Say what is unknown rather than give a result because a week has passed.

sections.title: One fitting step
items: Take one fitting step after the review. Make the contact, prepare the sexual boundary, or maintain what’s already working. You can save a group or service to try when personal contact isn’t available.
The step doesn’t need to remove desire or loneliness immediately. It should give the actual need some attention while keeping the behaviour you want to change clear.

question.prompt: What happened with the screen rule from Day 53?

opts.t: I followed it and it helped when I needed it
I followed it but it didn’t clearly help
It didn’t fit or interfered with essential use
I didn’t follow it
The situation didn’t happen or I don’t know the result

fb.lead: Keep a helpful part or change what didn’t fit.
items: If you didn’t try it, make the beginning easier. If the situation hasn’t happened, check afterwards.

practice: Review the Day 53 screen rule: did you follow it, did it help, and what should stay or change? Keep the check for after use if you haven’t tried it.
Then take a fitting step: focused time with a willing person, an invitation, a regular contact option, or checking the Day 21 sexual boundary. If no need is present, maintain something useful.
lessons.doneWhen: The rule is reviewed or rescheduled, and the chosen step is taken. Sex, disclosure, and another person’s reply aren’t required.

lessons.title: Follow up on a connection

openingQuote.text: The only way to have a friend is to be one.

closingQuote.text: Friendship is a sheltering tree.

sections.title: Another meeting
items: Relationships usually need another meeting after the first good conversation. A reasonable follow-up gives the connection a chance to continue.
Choose someone or somewhere you already know. Suggest a specific activity, ask about the next group session, or attend again.
You don’t need to create an impressive social plan. Repeating a shared activity can be enough.

Give the other person space to choose. If they’ve declined or contact remains one-sided, stop pressing and look elsewhere. Respecting a boundary is a useful action, even when the answer disappoints you.

sections.title: Make it easy to return
items: If you’re returning to a group, check the details that might prevent attendance: time, transport, cost, or accessibility.
Prepare what you can. The practical beginning matters more than promising to become more outgoing.
Suppose you met someone at a class and enjoyed talking. “Would you like to get a coffee after next week’s session?” gives them something clear to answer.
A message needn’t include your full recovery story or a request for deep friendship.

When another person is busy, keep other parts of life moving. You can enjoy a hobby, make another appropriate plan, or rest while waiting. One person’s availability doesn’t decide whether the evening has value.

sections.title: One follow-up
items: If safe contacts are scarce, a recurring group or service may be a better starting point than trying to force closeness with someone unsuitable. Check how to join and take the first step you can.
Today, make one follow-up, attend, or register. A reply isn’t required for completion. If a clear boundary means the right action is leaving someone space, identify a different option instead.
Afterwards, remember what helped you take part and what would make returning easier. Then let the relationship be a relationship.
It doesn’t need to become another daily score or carry every difficulty you’re working through.

practice: Make one reasonable follow-up with a person or group you know. Suggest an activity, ask about the next session, register, or attend again.
If someone has declined or contact is one-sided, leave them space and choose another option. Check timing, cost, and access where needed.
lessons.doneWhen: You’ve followed up or attended. Respecting a clear boundary and finding another suitable option also counts.

lessons.title: Set a safe limit on harmful contact

openingQuote.text: Associate with people who are likely to improve you.

closingQuote.text: Show me your friends, and I’ll show you your future.

sections.title: Contact that makes it harder
items: Some contact makes the behaviour you want to change harder. A group may repeatedly send explicit material, ignore a stated limit, or pressure you to join activities you’ve chosen to stop.
Writer and former boxer Ed Latimore has described changes in his social life after stopping drinking.
His account includes how relationships fitted differently with sobriety. It’s his own account, not evidence that every friendship should end when someone changes a habit.

sections.title: A proportionate limit
items: Look at a specific interaction. What happens repeatedly? What limit have you chosen? Which part can you control safely?
You might mute a channel, decline an invitation, leave a conversation, or ask for support before making a larger decision.
Don’t turn a disagreement or one awkward evening into a diagnosis of the person. Describe the behaviour and choose a proportionate response.
“I won’t stay in a group that keeps sending material I’ve asked not to receive” is clearer than a broad label about bad people.

sections.title: When safety comes first
items: Some situations involve danger, dependence, or coercion. Get appropriate support before acting, and avoid confrontation alone when it could make you less safe.
The exercise doesn’t require leaving a home, job, or relationship today.
If there is no harmful interaction, keep or arrange time with someone you value.
You don’t need to find a bad relationship to make the lesson applicable. When personal contact is unavailable, check a suitable group or service instead.

sections.title: One safe change
items: Today, make one safe change or take one support step. Save the limit in your plan only if you’ll need to remember it later. Another person’s agreement isn’t required for a boundary about your own action.
The useful question is whether the contact respects the choices you’re making and the wellbeing of the people involved. Work from repeated facts, with enough help for the size of the decision.

practice: If an interaction repeatedly causes harm or ignores your limit, choose one safe change: mute a channel, limit your availability, decline an invitation, or seek support before acting.
Save your own action if you’ll need to remember it. If no harmful interaction fits, keep or arrange time with someone you value, or check a support setting when contact isn’t available.
lessons.doneWhen: You’ve made a safe change, taken a support step, or maintained a healthy connection. Confrontation isn’t required.

lessons.title: Give a relationship attention

openingQuote.text: Friendship is a single soul dwelling in two bodies.

closingQuote.text: The better part of one’s life consists of his friendships.

sections.title: Attention through action
items: Give a good relationship attention through something you do. Listen, help, keep a plan, make a call, or apologise where an apology is needed.
Support doesn’t have to involve discussing porn. A meal together, a shared interest, or an ordinary conversation can matter.
If you want help with the behaviour, ask clearly and check whether the person is willing and able to offer it.
Be careful about making one person your only answer. They may be busy, need limits, or lack the expertise for a serious difficulty.
Keep appropriate services available as well. A friendship and professional care can have different roles.

sections.title: Review the four sessions
items: Today, review the four activity opportunities scheduled on Day 35. What actually happened?
Did you attend, enjoy it, or encounter the same obstacle? Decide whether the activity deserves a continuing place or needs a change.
If some sessions are still ahead, keep their reviews for afterwards. Four dates on a calendar aren’t four completed sessions. Record what you know and leave the rest pending.

sections.title: One relationship step
items: Then take one relationship step. Keep an existing commitment if it’s useful.
If you send an invitation or apology, make it appropriate and allow the other person to answer in their own time. Completion doesn’t depend on a reply or forgiveness.
If no safe relationship is available, take a step towards a suitable group or service. Check attendance or contact details so the option is more than a name on a list.

sections.title: Its own value
items: Let the action have its own value. Helping someone isn’t a bargain that obliges them to help you later. Listening doesn’t require them to solve your problem.
The relationship can be part of a fuller week without becoming a technique you use only when an urge appears.
Keep whatever regular contact has been useful, with limits that both people can understand and respect.

practice: Review the four Day 35 activity opportunities. Record what happened and whether to continue. Keep checks for any future sessions after they occur.
Then do one useful thing for a relationship: listen, help, keep a plan, attempt a call, or make an appropriate apology or invitation.
If no safe relationship is available, take a step towards a group or service.
lessons.doneWhen: The activity review is recorded or kept for later, and you’ve taken one relationship or support step.

lessons.title: Choose support without revisiting painful events

openingQuote.text: The child is father of the man.

closingQuote.text: It is never too late to be what you might have been.

sections.title: The present-day reaction
items: Past experiences may affect how you respond now, but this course can’t tell you what caused a current reaction. You don’t need to describe painful events to work on a present-day need.
If a connection to the past seems relevant, choose a reaction you can name today: becoming tense in an argument, withdrawing, or wanting to escape a difficult feeling.
Then choose a safe response for the present. You might orient yourself to the room, step away from an unsafe interaction, or contact someone appropriate.
Keep the reflection optional. You can skip it without a reason. If it becomes upsetting, stop and choose ordinary care or support.
There is no requirement to write a detailed account, revisit a memory, or prove you have found the root of porn use.

sections.title: What a course can’t provide
items: Structured trauma treatments have trained clinicians, defined procedures, and support.
For example, written exposure therapy described by the US Department of Veterans Affairs is a therapist-led treatment. A daily journaling exercise shouldn’t pretend to provide the same thing.
Suppose conflict makes you want to disappear into browsing. Today you could close the content, notice where you are, and decide when or with whom to discuss the conflict safely.
You can address that reaction without tracing it back through your entire history.
If no connection fits, say the topic doesn’t apply and continue the day. Not every habit needs a childhood explanation. The practical steps you’ve already prepared remain available.

sections.title: Care now
items: Today’s task is to prepare one present-day support option, or choose to skip. Use a gentle grounding action only if it’s comfortable. If the problem feels too distressing to manage alone, seek qualified help.
You don’t need to finish understanding the past before taking care of yourself now. Food, rest, safety, and appropriate support are available reasons for the next action.

practice: This exercise is optional. You can name one present-day reaction and prepare a safe response, such as noticing the room, leaving an unsafe setting, or saving a qualified support contact.
Try gentle grounding only if comfortable.
You can also mark the topic as not relevant or skip without giving a reason. If reflection becomes upsetting, stop and choose care or support. No account of a past event is required.
lessons.doneWhen: A present-day response is prepared, or you’ve chosen to skip, stop, or mark the topic not relevant.

lessons.title: Change one difficult setting

openingQuote.text: You are the average of the five people you spend the most time with.

closingQuote.text: The first step toward getting somewhere is to decide that you are not going to stay where you are.

sections.title: What keeps happening
items: Change one part of the setting that keeps making your difficult evenings harder. Start with something you control safely.

It may be a browsing routine, the place you work, a late-night conversation, or an account that keeps sending material you don’t want. Describe what happens repeatedly, then choose a proportionate change.
For example, working in bed might leave the laptop open when you’re tired. You could finish the specified work at a table and put the device away afterwards.
If the table isn’t available, close the work and change how the device is stored. Fit the action to the space you have.

sections.title: Proportionate changes
items: A contact may need a limit rather than a dramatic break. You might mute a channel or decline one kind of invitation.
If the situation is unsafe or complicated, get support before making a change. This lesson doesn’t require leaving a relationship, home, or job.
Avoid making a broad life decision from one difficult night. Look at the repeated facts and what you’ve already tried.
Sometimes the missing change is small; sometimes the problem needs advice, care, or more resources than a course can provide.

sections.title: Start today
items: Choose the first action and do it today if possible. If support must come first, make the enquiry.
If the setting can’t be changed immediately, prepare a response you can use within it, without blaming yourself for the constraint.
There may be no relevant setting to change. Keep what’s helping and record that no adjustment is needed. The calendar reaching a new lesson isn’t evidence that another rule is necessary.
After a chance to use the change, check whether it addressed the specific problem. Don’t ask whether your whole life is fixed.
Knowing that work now ends before browsing begins, or that a harmful channel is muted, gives you a clearer result to build on.

practice: Choose one setting that repeatedly makes difficult evenings harder, if any. Change a feature you safely control: timing, device use, work location, or contact with a harmful channel.
If changing it is unsafe or complicated, request support first. If nothing fits, keep what’s helping and record that no change is needed.
lessons.doneWhen: You’ve made a safe adjustment or support step, or confirmed no change is needed. Leaving a home, job, or relationship isn’t required.

lessons.title: Describe a mistake without an insult

openingQuote.text: No one can make you feel inferior without your consent.

closingQuote.text: The greatest discovery of my generation is that a human being can alter his life by altering his attitudes.

sections.title: Criticism or insult

items.t: “I missed the deadline.”
“I’m useless.”

items: Separate useful criticism from an insult. “I missed the deadline” names an event. “I’m useless” makes a claim about the whole person.
Write the event, its consequence, and what needs attention. Keep responsibility in the sentence. If work was delayed, say so and choose the next step.
If an agreement was broken, consider the appropriate repair. Removing the insult doesn’t erase either.

sections.title: Speaking to yourself
items: Research by Ethan Kross and colleagues tested ways of speaking to oneself under stress.
In several experiments, using one’s name or non-first-person language affected responses to stressful tasks. This isn’t a treatment test for porn use.
You can try the idea if it makes a factual response easier: “Alex missed the task. What’s the next step?” Use your own name, or ordinary first-person wording if that feels more natural.

The sentence shouldn’t become a performance. “I watched longer than planned. I’ll close it now and prepare for bed” is enough. You don’t need to convince yourself you’re wonderful before taking the action.

sections.title: Keep the fact
items: Choose a recent judgement if one is available. What part is a fact, and what part is a sweeping conclusion? Keep the fact and remove the unsupported claim. Save the short response for Day 68.
If there is no harsh judgement today, describe an everyday difficulty plainly or mark the exercise as unnecessary. Don’t invent a mistake to practise being kinder.

sections.title: Then act
items: Then return to something useful. Take the repair step, meet a basic need, or ask for support. Rewriting the sentence repeatedly can become another way to postpone the action.

If self-criticism is severe, persistent, or linked to serious distress, seek qualified help. A factual sentence can help with a moment; it isn’t expected to carry every problem behind how you speak to yourself.

practice: Choose a recent harsh judgement if available. Write the event, actual consequence, and next action without the insult or unsupported claim about yourself.
Save the brief response for Day 68. Include a repair or support step if needed. If no harsh judgement fits, describe an everyday difficulty factually or mark the task unnecessary.
lessons.doneWhen: You’ve written the factual response or recorded that the pattern doesn’t apply. No new mistake is needed.

lessons.title: When you feel bad about yourself

openingQuote.text: Hatred is blind.

closingQuote.text: Nothing is more deceitful than the appearance of humility. It is often only carelessness of opinion, and sometimes an indirect boast.

sections.title: When it feels pointless
items: Self-loathing can make an action feel pointless before you begin it. You may avoid a meal, a conversation, or work because the judgement says you don’t deserve another attempt.
Bring the judgement back to what you know. “I did something I regret” leaves room for a repair. “Everything about me is bad” goes beyond the event and gives you no instructions for what to do next.
Use yesterday’s factual response if it fits. Then choose one action the judgement has been preventing: eat, wash, keep a commitment, make appropriate contact, or ask for professional support.
The action can begin while the feeling remains.

sections.title: Ordinary contact
items: Suppose you watched longer than planned and now don’t want to answer a friend. You can reply about the plan you made without disclosing the entire episode.
The friend isn’t owed a confession, and you aren’t required to feel good about yourself before keeping ordinary contact.

If a real repair is needed, make it proportionate. An apology should address the person affected. It shouldn’t become a request that they reassure you repeatedly or take responsibility for the next attempt.
There may be no self-loathing problem today. Continue one normal act of care and leave the analysis aside. A course about this topic doesn’t need to make the topic part of every reader’s identity.

sections.title: Take the action once
items: Take the chosen action once. Afterwards, notice whether it helped you resume something important.
Don’t demand that it remove the judgement immediately. The meal or appointment can matter even while your thoughts remain harsh.
When self-hatred is persistent or overwhelming, get qualified support. If you’re in immediate danger, use urgent local help.
You can work on the behaviour you want to change while also receiving care for distress that deserves attention in its own right.

practice: Use the Day 66 example if it fits. Bring a broad judgement back to the facts and take one action it has been preventing: food, washing, a commitment, appropriate contact, or professional support.
If no such judgement fits, keep normal care and leave the analysis aside. Disclosure is optional and should be appropriate to the person and situation.
lessons.doneWhen: You’ve taken the fitting action or requested support.

lessons.title: Check your response to self-criticism

openingQuote.text: Be kind, for everyone you meet is fighting a hard battle.

closingQuote.text: If you want others to be happy, practice compassion. If you want to be happy, practice compassion.

sections.title: A practical response
items: Self-compassion can be a practical response after a difficult moment. Describe what happened accurately, take care of what is needed, and choose a next step.
The experiments on Day 44 found that brief self-compassion exercises sometimes increased motivation to improve or make amends.
The lesson doesn’t require a warm feeling towards yourself. It asks whether the response helps you act without adding unnecessary punishment.

sections.title: Review your sentence
items: Review the sentence you wrote on Day 66. Did you use it? What happened next? Perhaps you ate, stopped browsing, or made a repair.
Perhaps you kept repeating the insult. Keep the result honest and adjust one detail if needed.
If you haven’t needed the response yet, read it once and name when you’d use it. That checks whether the wording is easy to remember.
It doesn’t show how it will help in a real difficult moment. Don’t create a mistake to get that information.

If self-criticism isn’t relevant, review the ordinary steps after a slip instead. The factual beginning might be enough: close the content, put the device away, and return to the next thing the hour needs.

sections.title: Make it easy to use
items: Keep the practice brief. If reflection makes you more distressed or turns into repeated checking, stop and choose an action or support. You don’t need a long account of why you feel the way you do.
Imagine saying the sentence after a tiring evening. Does it tell you what to do first?
If it’s full of reassuring claims you don’t believe, make it simpler. “That happened. I can put the phone away now” may be easier to use.
Today, finish with the next action rather than another paragraph about kindness.
Food, rest, repair, and appropriate help can be taken seriously without requiring you to settle every judgement about yourself first.

question.prompt: What happened when you used the Day 66 response?

opts.t: It helped me begin the next action
I used it but it didn’t clearly help
The wording or next action didn’t fit
I haven’t needed it yet
Self-criticism isn’t a problem for me

fb.lead: Keep what helped or change one awkward detail.
items: If you haven’t needed it, practise the short response once. If the topic doesn’t fit, keep the after-slip steps instead.

practice: Review a real use of the Day 66 response if there has been one. Record what happened next and change one detail if needed.
If you haven’t needed it, read it once and name when you’d use it. If self-criticism doesn’t fit, check the after-slip steps instead. Keep this brief and stop if reflection becomes upsetting.
lessons.doneWhen: You’ve reviewed actual use or practised a suitable response without creating a mistake.

lessons.title: Keep one manageable commitment

openingQuote.text: Trust thyself: every heart vibrates to that iron string.

closingQuote.text: Well done is better than well said.

sections.title: Small enough to attempt
items: Choose a commitment small enough to attempt today. Give it a time or cue, prepare what it needs, and see what happens.
Use something useful: a short hobby session, an easy meal, a first piece of work, or a device rule that’s helping. You can keep an existing commitment rather than add another task.
Suppose you want to read after dinner. Put the book beside the chair and decide to read a few pages before the feed.
The promise is specific enough to follow and modest enough to fit a normal evening. If you’re unwell, rest may be the better commitment.

sections.title: Completed, changed, or missed
items: Afterwards, record completed, changed, or missed. If you changed it, say why.
If you missed it, ask what got in the way: forgetting, time, unavailable materials, or an activity that didn’t fit. Then choose the next reasonable chance.

A missed attempt doesn’t need extra punishment. Adding an hour of work to tomorrow may make the commitment even harder. A visible reminder or a smaller beginning may address the problem more directly.
Nor does one completed task establish that you’ll keep every future promise. Let the evidence stay the size it is.
You attempted this action and saw this result. Repeating useful commitments can give you more to rely on over time.

sections.title: Keep it simple
items: Keep the notes short. If recording becomes more demanding than the activity, simplify the record. The point is to understand whether the plan fits, then spend time doing it.
Today, make the attempt and decide what follows. You don’t have to announce a new identity or wait to feel fully trustworthy.
A clear action, an honest result, and another reasonable opportunity are enough to work with.
If the plan repeatedly fails because a larger difficulty is unresolved, ask for help with that difficulty rather than keep lowering your opinion of yourself.

practice: Choose one useful, modest action and give it a time or cue. Prepare the materials and attempt it. An existing commitment is fine.
Record completed, changed, or missed, with a practical reason if needed. If missed, choose the next realistic chance without adding punishment or restarting the course.
lessons.doneWhen: You’ve made the attempt and recorded the result, including an appropriate adjustment.

lessons.title: Simplify the plan

openingQuote.text: Waste no more time arguing what a good man should be. Be one.

closingQuote.text: Become who you are.

sections.title: What the course has added
items: Review what the course has added to your day. Keep the parts you can explain and use. Simplify the ones that have become more demanding than helpful.

You may have a phone rule, a response to urges, an activity, a few notes, and review reminders. Each should serve a purpose. You don’t need a large collection of techniques to prove you’re making an effort.
Ask which change has actually helped. Keep it. Ask which one has an awkward beginning. Make that beginning easier. If an optional task gives you no useful information or action, consider stopping it.

sections.title: Cut what isn’t helping
items: Suppose nightly tracking now takes half an hour and leads to repeated checking. A brief note about whether the phone stayed out of bed may be enough.
The record should help you make decisions without taking the evening it’s meant to protect.
Or perhaps the activity schedule contains more sessions than you can attend. Keep the one you value and can realistically repeat. Missing the other sessions isn’t a reason to abandon the useful one.
If everything has a clear purpose and fits, leave it alone. The exercise doesn’t require deleting a task just to produce an answer. You can confirm the plan is manageable.

sections.title: A plan for a busy evening
items: Keep professional care separate from optional course demands. Discuss treatment changes with the relevant clinician. A lesson about simplifying isn’t advice to stop prescribed care or medication.
Today, leave a plan you could use on a normal, busy evening. Put the first actions where you’ll find them. Retain review dates that will help with an actual decision.
Then use some of the time for the rest of life. You don’t need to make self-improvement the new activity that fills every gap.
The course should support sleep, work, pleasure, relationships, and care, rather than become another thing that repeatedly crowds them out.

practice: Review your plan. Keep something that helps, simplify something awkward if needed, and stop an optional demand only if it has no useful purpose.
If every part fits, retain it. Discuss changes to professional treatment with the clinician; don’t treat it as an optional course demand. Leave a plan you can explain and use on a busy evening.
lessons.doneWhen: The plan is reviewed and manageable. Another improvement project isn’t required.

lessons.title: Use what your notes show

openingQuote.text: Know thyself.
openingQuote.by: Inscription at the Temple of Apollo at Delphi

closingQuote.text: To know oneself is the beginning of wisdom.

sections.title: Read a few entries
items: Read two or three entries from your plan. Choose ones that contain something you can use: what happened before browsing, a response you tried, or an activity you attended.
Look for a repeated difficulty and a response that helped. If the record doesn’t support either, say so.
A few entries aren’t enough to explain your whole personality, and you don’t need a tidy pattern to continue.
Perhaps the same problem appears after late shifts. Food and an earlier stopping time may be worth preparing.
Perhaps you keep the phone rule easily but avoid the work waiting afterwards. That points towards the task itself, not another charger location.

sections.title: Adjust the week
items: Use the information to adjust the coming week. Keep the change that’s helping and work on the detail that keeps getting in the way. One adjustment is easier to assess than a complete redesign.
If the notes are thin, choose one observation to collect next week. You could record when searching begins, whether the phone stays out of bed, or what happens after an urge.
Pick the information you’ll need for a decision. Unknown is a valid answer until you have it.
Keep the device placement and rules that help. You don’t need to keep changing them because a lesson asks you to review. Confirming that they still fit can be the result.

sections.title: When you need more help
items: If the record shows worsening control or serious effects on daily life, use that information to seek qualified help. Understanding yourself includes recognising when the current level of support isn’t enough.
Today, make the week’s plan reflect what you actually know. Then begin one useful action from it.
Save only the notes that will help you remember or review. A plan that you can read and follow is more useful than a lengthy explanation you rarely open.

practice: Read two or three useful entries. Identify one repeated difficulty and one response that helped if the record supports them. Use that information for the coming week.
If the record is thin, choose one brief observation to collect instead. Keep the existing setup when it fits, and take a support step if the record shows the current help isn’t enough.
lessons.doneWhen: The week reflects actual information or a focused plan to gather it.

lessons.title: Choose what you can do now

openingQuote.text: My formula for greatness in a human being is amor fati: that one wants nothing to be different.

closingQuote.text: The willing are led by fate, the reluctant dragged.

sections.title: Accepting what happened
items: You can’t undo a past decision. You may still be able to repair a consequence or decide what happens next.
The Stoic idea often called amor fati can be read as accepting that the event has happened. Epictetus discusses responding to events we can’t fully control.
You don’t have to welcome harm, excuse another person’s behaviour, or feel grateful for a painful experience to take a present action.

head: Already settled
Still within reach
rows: An apology and a new booking

items: Choose an everyday event if this reflection is useful. What is already settled? What remains within reach? A missed appointment might allow an apology and a new booking.
A lost evening might allow food and sleep now. Some things have no direct repair, and continuing a valued activity may be the next step.

sections.title: Gratitude is optional
items: Gratitude is a separate option, not an obligation. Emmons and McCullough tested gratitude-focused diary exercises and found benefits for some measures, but not every outcome improved in every study.
Those findings don’t require thanking someone who harmed you or making every setback into a lesson.
If you’d like, notice something you appreciate in the present. Keep it specific: a person who helped, a meal, or a place you can rest. If gratitude feels forced, leave it aside.
The reflection is also optional. You can skip it if it becomes upsetting or unhelpful. Choose ordinary care or appropriate support instead. There’s no reason to retell a painful event for the course.

sections.title: One proportionate action
items: Today, take one proportionate action. Make the repair, begin an activity, or ask for help. Let that action end the reflection for now.

Acceptance doesn’t need to settle how you feel about the past. It can simply mean working from what has happened, without repeatedly waiting for a different past before using the choices available today.

question.prompt: Which meaning of acceptance fits the lesson?

opts.t: I have to feel grateful for every harmful event
I can recognise what happened and take a fitting action now, without approving the harm
I must contact everyone involved in a regret

best.t: I can recognise what happened and take a fitting action now, without approving the harm

items: You can take an appropriate next step and respect boundaries. Skip the reflection if it’s upsetting or unhelpful.

practice: If helpful, choose an everyday past event and distinguish what has happened from what you can do now. Take a proportionate repair or present-day action.
If no repair fits, choose a valued activity. If reflection is upsetting or unhelpful, skip and choose care or support. Gratitude, forgiveness, and retelling a painful event aren’t required.
lessons.doneWhen: You’ve taken a fitting action or chosen to skip the reflection.

lessons.title: Reserve time for what matters

openingQuote.text: You could leave life right now. Let that determine what you do and say and think.

closingQuote.text: It is not death that a man should fear, but he should fear never beginning to live.

sections.title: Make room this week
items: What have you been meaning to give more time to? A person, a skill, an enjoyable activity, or a responsibility may come to mind.
The question “What if I had five years left?” can help some people choose.
For others, thinking about mortality is upsetting or unnecessary. You can use a simpler question: what do I want to make room for this week?

sections.title: Reserve a block
items: Choose one answer and reserve a realistic block in the next seven days. An hour may fit; fifteen minutes may be more honest.
If another person is involved, make an invitation and allow them to choose. If a booking is needed, check the details.
Suppose you keep saying you’d like to see an old friend. Suggest a day and an activity rather than write “relationships” as a goal.
If the person isn’t available, choose another date or a different valued activity. Their reply isn’t something the course can require.

Begin a small part today: prepare materials, send the invitation, or make the booking. The future block should have a practical beginning rather than depend on becoming a different kind of person first.

sections.title: Check afterwards
items: Set a check for after the block. Did it happen? Did it fit? Would you give it time again? We’ll revisit it on Day 84 if it’s occurred by then. Otherwise, leave the reminder for after the actual session.
You can reuse something already in the week. The task doesn’t require a dramatic new priority. Keeping a commitment to someone you value may be enough.
When the block arrives, give it your attention as far as circumstances allow. If something interrupts it, record that and choose another chance.
The purpose is to make time for what matters, without turning a missed appointment into another reason to abandon the plan.

practice: Choose a person, activity, or responsibility you want to give more time to. Reserve a realistic block in the next seven days and begin a small part today, or make the needed invitation or booking.
Set a review after the block: did it happen, did it fit, and will you repeat it? Save it for Day 84 if due then, or for after the actual session.
lessons.doneWhen: The time and review are scheduled and a first step is taken. Mortality reflection is optional.

lessons.title: Begin an activity you postponed

openingQuote.text: Carpe diem, quam minimum credula postero.

closingQuote.text: While we are postponing, life speeds by.

sections.title: Ten to twenty minutes
items: Begin a part of the activity you’ve been postponing. Use yesterday’s choice if it fits.
Choose ten to twenty minutes of something available today. Read, practise, walk, prepare a meal, or make a necessary enquiry.
If the activity depends on another person or booking, make that arrangement and prepare what you can.

sections.title: Enough to begin
items: It’s easy to keep preparation going indefinitely. You look for the best book, the right equipment, or a more convenient week.
Ask whether you already have enough to begin the first small part. Sometimes another purchase or plan isn’t what is missing.
Suppose you want to learn guitar and have an instrument at home. A short session with a lesson you already have is a beginning.
You can decide about better equipment after you’ve tried it. If you lack access to the activity, checking a class or borrowing option may be today’s first step.

sections.title: Using the day quietly
items: The phrase carpe diem is often used to urge dramatic living. Here, the day can be used quietly.
Keeping a planned meal with someone or deliberately resting after a demanding week may be the right choice. Productivity isn’t the only way to spend time well.
If there is no postponed activity, keep an existing enjoyable commitment. There is no need to invent an ambition because the course is approaching its end.

sections.title: After the first session
items: After beginning, notice what you need for another session. Make one practical adjustment or leave things as they are. You don’t have to convert the activity into a strict programme today.
The first session may be awkward or less exciting than expected. Let the result tell you something about the activity, rather than treat it as a verdict on your future.
You’ve begun, and you now have more information for the next choice.

practice: Begin ten to twenty minutes of something you want more of, using the Day 73 choice if it fits. If another person or booking is needed, make the arrangement and prepare what you can.
If no postponed activity fits, keep an enjoyable commitment or deliberately rest. The task doesn’t require productivity or a reply.
lessons.doneWhen: You’ve begun, made the needed arrangement, or kept a fitting commitment.

lessons.title: Plan the next ninety days

openingQuote.text: Plans are nothing; planning is everything.

closingQuote.text: Give me six hours to chop down a tree and I will spend the first four sharpening the axe.

sections.title: One aim
items: Choose one aim for the next ninety days. Give it a weekly action, a smaller version for difficult weeks, and dates to check how it’s going.
Rich Roll’s biography describes entering rehabilitation at thirty-one and making major fitness changes around forty. Those events happened years apart.
Compressing them into one dramatic transformation would misrepresent his story. His elite sporting achievements also aren’t a useful standard for your next three months.
Use the story as a reminder that help and later changes can have different places in a life.
Choose an aim that fits yours: attending a regular group, learning a skill, improving a sleep routine, or following through on appropriate care.

sections.title: A weekly action
items: Write the action clearly. “Walk with a friend on Saturday” or “attend the Tuesday class” gives the week something definite. You can reuse the activity from Day 35 if it still matters.
Schedule the next four chances and begin one small part today. If another person is needed, make the invitation or booking and prepare what you control. A reply isn’t required to take the first step.

sections.title: Reviews, not deadlines
items: Set reviews after two weeks and at thirty, sixty, and ninety days. Ask whether you attended, what helped, and what needs changing.
These are times to look at results, not deadlines by which you must feel recovered.
Write a smaller version for a difficult week and how you’ll resume after interruption. A ten-minute session or the next available class may fit better than restarting the entire plan.

Keep the aim to one thing for now. You can continue other helpful routines without declaring them all new goals. The plan should be easy enough to follow when the enthusiasm from today’s lesson has worn off.

question.prompt: What are the next ninety days for?

opts.t: A universal deadline for brain recovery
Time to practise one weekly action and check how it goes
A test that allows no change for illness or responsibilities

best.t: Time to practise one weekly action and check how it goes

items: Try the scheduled sessions and review what fits; the date doesn’t promise a transformation.

practice: Choose one aim for ninety days and a realistic weekly action. Schedule four chances, then begin a small part or make the needed arrangement today.
Set reviews after two weeks and at thirty, sixty, and ninety days. Write a smaller version for difficult weeks and how you’ll resume after interruption. You can reuse an existing activity.
lessons.doneWhen: The aim, dates, reviews, smaller version, and first step are saved or completed.

lessons.title: Give one activity your attention

openingQuote.text: No man is more unhappy than he who never faces adversity. For he is not permitted to prove himself.

closingQuote.text: Nothing can bring you peace but yourself.

sections.title: One interruption
items: Choose one input that keeps interrupting time you want for something else. It might be a feed, notifications, news, or a particular conversation.
Set it aside for twenty to thirty minutes at a time you’d normally use it. Keep essential calls, care, work, and accessibility available.
Decide what receives the attention instead: a meal, a person, a hobby, or rest.
Suppose you’re eating while checking several feeds. Try finishing the meal without unrelated switching.
You don’t have to make the room silent or pretend the feeds are harmful in every setting. You’re checking whether this limit improves this part of the day.

sections.title: When it’s a person
items: If the input is a person, choose a respectful boundary about your own availability.
Reply later when appropriate, or ask to speak at another time. Don’t use the exercise to ignore urgent care or an agreement you need to keep.

sections.title: Afterwards
items: At the end, ask what happened. Did you give the chosen activity more attention? Did you simply switch to another distraction?
Was the limit helpful, awkward, or unnecessary? Keep the answer factual rather than claim that the mind has become permanently peaceful.
If no input is causing difficulty, deliberately choose an enjoyable activity and give it the time. You don’t need to find something to remove.
Decide whether to repeat the limit. A specific rule for a meal or work block may fit better than trying to control every interruption all day. If it didn’t help, adjust or leave it aside.
Peace of mind can be an appealing aim, but a course task can’t guarantee it. Today’s smaller question is whether one chosen part of life receives the attention you intended.
That gives you something you can try again without requiring a particular mood first.

practice: Set aside one distracting feed, notification source, or other input for twenty to thirty minutes when you’d normally use it.
Keep essential functions and commitments available. Choose what gets your attention instead.
Record whether the limit helped and whether to repeat it. If no input fits, give an enjoyable activity the time without unrelated switching.
lessons.doneWhen: You’ve tried the limit or chosen activity and recorded the result. Silence or feeling calmer isn’t required.

lessons.title: Schedule something you want to keep doing

openingQuote.text: The future depends on what you do today.

closingQuote.text: The best way to predict your future is to create it.

sections.title: A normal day next year
items: Imagine a normal day a year from now. Choose one recurring activity you’d like to be part of it, rather than picture a life with no difficult moments.

You might want a class in the week, time with someone, a hobby, or a routine that protects sleep. Give the activity real dates now. You can reuse the opportunities from Day 35 or Day 75 when they fit.

sections.title: Four chances and two checks
items: Schedule four chances and make the first practical step: invitation, booking, or preparation.
If the activity requires another person, give them a clear choice and prepare something you can do while waiting for an answer.
Set a review after the first session and another after four weeks. What happened? Was it worth the time? Is the schedule realistic?
A future picture is useful when it helps you try something, not when it gives you another ideal to compare yourself against.
Suppose you imagine belonging to a running group. Check the actual meeting time and whether the pace and location suit you. Register or ask a question.
If running doesn’t fit, choose another regular shared activity. The point is the life you want to build, not a particular hobby.

sections.title: Expect changes
items: We’ll check the first session on Day 84 if it has occurred by then. If it hasn’t, keep the reminder for afterwards. You don’t need to speed up the schedule to produce a result for the final lesson.

Expect changes. Work, health, and other people’s availability may alter the dates. Make a reasonable adjustment and continue rather than take the interruption as proof the year is already going wrong.
Today, leave the activity with dates, a first step, and two checks. Then let it be something you do and experience. It doesn’t need to remain an image of a more impressive future self.

practice: Name one recurring activity you’d like in life a year from now. Schedule four chances, or confirm dates already made on Day 35 or 75. Make the first invitation, booking, or preparation.
Set a review after the first session and another after four weeks. Add the first to Day 84 if it’s happened by then; otherwise keep the later reminder.
lessons.doneWhen: The activity has dates, a first step, and both review reminders.

lessons.title: Keep the reason and next action clear

openingQuote.text: The whole future lies in uncertainty: live immediately.

closingQuote.text: How long are you going to wait before you demand the best for yourself?

sections.title: Your reason, revisited
items: You don’t have to decide how every year ahead will go before following your rule today. Keep the long-term reason clear and the next action manageable.

Read the reason you wrote on Day 13. Does it still fit? Perhaps protecting sleep remains the main aim. Perhaps your experience has made another consequence clearer. Rewrite the reason plainly if needed.
“I want to stop losing evenings to searching” is enough. You don’t need a promise that urges will never return or that every future day will be easy.
A personal or religious choice can also be stated without turning guilt alone into a diagnosis.

sections.title: One behaviour for ninety days
items: Choose one useful behaviour to keep for the next ninety days. It might be putting the phone away at bedtime, following a first response, or keeping a regular activity.
Use something that has helped, rather than the strictest rule you can imagine.
Give it a review date. You can reuse a check already scheduled on Day 75.
The review is a chance to see whether the behaviour remains useful and whether the support needs changing. It isn’t automatic permission to abandon your porn boundary.
Use the behaviour today when its cue appears. If it doesn’t, practise the first step without an urge and leave what you need ready. Don’t create a risky situation to test the promise.

sections.title: Keep it where you’ll find it
items: If the course hasn’t helped enough, the long-term decision may include qualified care.
Making a request for help is compatible with keeping the reason you started. You don’t need to wait for one more difficult night to justify it.
Save the reason, behaviour, and date where you’ll find them after the course ends. Keep the wording brief enough to read on a tired evening.
A future commitment is easier to use when it tells you what to do next, rather than ask you to settle the rest of your life at once.

practice: Keep or rewrite the reason from Day 13 under Goal. Choose one behaviour that has helped to keep for ninety days and save a review date. You can reuse a date from Day 75.
Use the behaviour today when its cue occurs. Otherwise practise the first step and keep the setup ready. Don’t create a risky test.
lessons.doneWhen: The reason and review are saved, and the behaviour is used or its first step practised.

lessons.title: Compare the start with now

openingQuote.text: No man ever steps in the same river twice, for it is not the same river and he is not the same man.

closingQuote.text: The years teach much which the days never know.

sections.title: Then and now
items: Compare the start with now. Use the Day 1 notes or earliest entry you actually have. If you’re relying on memory, say so and keep the claims cautious.
Look at time spent watching, effects on daily life, what happens during an urge, and what happens after a slip.
Include an activity or routine if you’ve been trying one. Mark unchanged, worse, or unknown when those are the accurate answers.

sections.title: Mixed results count
items: A mixed result can be useful. You may watch less but still lose sleep to another feed. You may stop sooner after a slip while urges remain frequent.
The next action depends on the difference, so don’t smooth it into a success story or dismiss it all as failure.
If the starting record is incomplete, you can’t manufacture missing numbers.
“I watched most evenings, but didn’t record the time” is a valid starting point. Begin a clearer observation now if it will help with a decision.

sections.title: One decision
items: Choose one decision from the comparison. Keep something that’s helping, adjust a weak part, or seek more support. You don’t need to change the whole plan at once.
Suppose the phone boundary has helped but the planned hobby rarely happens.
Keep the boundary and ask what prevents the hobby: timing, materials, or lack of interest. Those are different from a problem with the boundary itself.

sections.title: If things are worse
items: If control or daily life is worse, take that seriously. Contact a qualified professional rather than wait for the final lesson to produce a reassuring ending.
The course length doesn’t decide when help is appropriate.
Today, record the comparison and take a first step on the decision. Then leave the review for its next scheduled time.
Looking backwards should help the next week, without taking over the hours you’re trying to use differently.

question.prompt: Which statements fit the record you actually have?
question.instr: Choose all that fit. Choose F alone if it fits.

opts.t: I lost less time or daily life was less disrupted
A response became easier to begin
I gave an activity or relationship more time
Some things stayed the same
Some difficulties became worse
I can’t make a clear comparison
Another observation

items: Note what supports each answer and choose one next step. Missing entries don’t prove that urges or viewing were absent.

practice: Compare your actual starting notes with now: time or disruption from viewing, responses to urges and slips, and one routine or activity. If recalling the start, say so.
Include unchanged, worse, and unknown honestly. Choose one decision: keep a helpful change, adjust a weak one, or seek more support. Take its first step.
lessons.doneWhen: The comparison and next decision are recorded, with a fitting first action.

lessons.title: Prepare for a changed situation

openingQuote.text: We are what we repeatedly do.

closingQuote.text: Habit is a second nature.

sections.title: A changed setting
items: Check whether a response you use at home can fit a changed situation. Travel, a shared room, or an unavailable phone may remove the familiar setup.
Choose one response that has helped and one likely change. Work out the first action in that setting. If the phone can’t go on the usual shelf, where can it go?
If going outside isn’t possible, what indoor activity fits? If the app is unavailable, can you use a short paper note or remember the steps?

sections.title: Rehearse the whole response
items: Try the steps once without an urge. Practise the whole response you chose, including the next activity.
For urge surfing, that means the brief observation, ordinary breathing, and ending; opening and closing its page isn’t the same practice.
You don’t need a sensation or sexual thought to rehearse. The attempt checks whether you know what to do and whether it is practical in the changed setting.
Only later use during an urge can show how it helps there.

sections.title: One likely situation
items: Suppose you’re sharing a room while travelling. Leaving the device elsewhere may be difficult.
You could close the content, put the phone face down out of reach, and begin reading with the materials available. Keep needed calls or accessibility in mind when choosing the setup.
Save the changed first step briefly if it would be easy to forget. Don’t build a detailed plan for every place you might ever visit. One likely situation is enough for today.

sections.title: What it tells you
items: If no response has helped, prepare a more suitable support option instead. Check access and make an enquiry when help is needed now. Another rehearsal shouldn’t delay that.
The result is practical information about where and how to begin. You don’t need to claim that practice has changed your brain or made you immune to future urges to use what you’ve prepared.

question.prompt: You practised the steps in another room without an urge. What have you learned?

opts.t: Whether the steps and materials were ready there
What got in the way and how to change it
That the response will work during every future urge
That my brain has reset

best.t: Whether the steps and materials were ready there
What got in the way and how to change it

items: Practice checks preparation. Use during an urge gives different information; neither measures a brain reset.

practice: Choose a response that helped and a likely changed situation, such as travel, a shared room, or no phone. Prepare an accessible first step and practise the response once without an urge.
If you choose an urge exercise, practise its steps and ending. If no response has helped, check a more suitable support option and enquire if help is needed now.
lessons.doneWhen: You’ve checked the response in a changed situation or prepared and used the needed support option.

lessons.title: Use the changes that helped

openingQuote.text: Victorious warriors win first and then go to war.

closingQuote.text: The greatest victory is that which requires no battle.

sections.title: Up to three changes
items: Keep up to three changes that have actually helped. Choose from what you’ve used, not everything the course suggested.
You might keep a device rule, a first response, and a weekly activity. You might choose support and a sleep routine instead. The useful list depends on your experience.
Use the changes in today’s routine. Put the phone away at the time you chose, attend the activity, or follow the response when its cue appears.
If the cue doesn’t happen, practise the first step and leave it ready. Don’t manufacture an urge or mistake to complete the day.

sections.title: Easy to remember
items: Ask whether the beginning is easy to remember. A short note in the place where you need it may help more than a long folder of lessons.
If a device is unavailable, keep the most necessary instructions on paper or somewhere else you can reach.
Suppose the evening rule has worked for several weeks. You don’t need to replace it with something more impressive as the course ends. Keep using it and give the time to the rest of the evening.

If a change helped only because the circumstances were unusually easy, keep that uncertainty in mind. You can prepare for a likely difficult situation or seek more support without declaring the change useless.

sections.title: A short list
items: If none has helped, don’t make a list just to satisfy the exercise. Look at what’s missing and take a step towards qualified help. A complete course isn’t proof that the available support was sufficient.
Today’s practice is use or rehearsal, not simply installing a tool or moving an object. Those preparations matter when you follow through at the relevant time.

Leave yourself a short list with reasons you recognise. It should help you remember what to do when the lessons stop arriving, rather than become another collection of rules you feel obliged to maintain.

question.prompt: Which changes have actually helped?
question.instr: Choose all that fit. Choose G alone if it fits.

opts.t: Where I keep the device or how I limit access
A clear first response
Another activity or a regular session
A sleep routine or smaller plan for difficult days
Appropriate support
Something else
Nothing has clearly helped

fb.lead: Keep up to three actions from your answers and note when each helped.
items: If nothing helped, take a step towards other support instead of filling the list.

practice: Choose up to three changes that helped and use them in today’s routine: device placement, a response, an activity, a sleep rule, or support.
If a cue doesn’t occur, practise the first step rather than create a test. If nothing helped clearly, record what’s missing and take a step towards other support.
lessons.doneWhen: You’ve used or practised the chosen changes, or taken a support step. Preparation alone isn’t the whole task.

lessons.title: Check how to ask for help

openingQuote.text: Fall seven times, stand up eight.

closingQuote.text: Our greatest glory is not in never falling, but in rising every time we fall.

sections.title: Lessons from other addictions
items: Other addictions can offer useful parallels about access, support, and returning after setbacks. They also have differences in risk and treatment that shouldn’t be borrowed casually.
In a GamCare account, David describes returning to gambling after three years away from it. His later help included therapy, debt advice, family support, and self-exclusion.
It’s one person’s story. It shows several kinds of help addressing several kinds of difficulty, rather than one technique carrying everything.
NIDA’s guidance on substance use also describes renewed use as a possible reason to resume or modify treatment.
This isn’t proof that porn use and substance dependence are the same. Medication, withdrawal care, and other treatment decisions belong with appropriate professionals.

sections.title: Check your support details
items: For your plan, check how you would ask for help. Confirm a first contact or service and a backup. Both can be services when personal contacts aren’t safe or available.
Check the details: contact method, hours, cost or eligibility where relevant, and what kind of help is offered. A saved name isn’t enough if you can’t reach the service when you need it.

sections.title: The first request
items: Write the opening request in your own words if it helps.

“I’m having persistent difficulty controlling my porn use and it’s affecting sleep and work. Can I arrange an assessment?” gives the service a clear starting point. Share only what’s needed for the enquiry.
If help is needed now, send the request or make the call. Don’t leave a prepared message unsent because the course hasn’t ended.
A reply isn’t required for today’s action; use the backup if the first option is unavailable.

Keep the support details alongside your first response and after-slip steps. The plan can include things you do alone and help you receive. It doesn’t need to make independence the measure of success.

question.prompt: Which lesson can you carefully take from other addiction care?

opts.t: Every problem has the same risks, medication, and withdrawal advice
Check the plan and seek fitting help when difficulty returns
A previous good period means more help can’t be needed

best.t: Check the plan and seek fitting help when difficulty returns

items: Planning and support can offer parallels, while risks and treatment depend on the particular problem.

practice: Confirm a first support contact or service and a backup. Check details, access conditions, and how to begin the request. Both options can be services if personal contacts aren’t available.
Draft a short opening message if helpful. If support is needed now, send the enquiry or make the call. Use the backup when the first option is unavailable.
lessons.doneWhen: Support details are checked and any needed first request is made. Personal disclosure or a reply isn’t required.

lessons.title: Finish with an honest next step

openingQuote.text: Every new beginning comes from some other beginning’s end.

closingQuote.text: There are years that ask questions and years that answer.

sections.title: An honest observation
items: Read an early entry alongside a recent one. Choose one observation you can honestly take forward, including “no clear change” if that is what the record shows.
Perhaps you put the phone away more consistently, ended an episode sooner, or returned to an activity you value.
Perhaps the same difficulty remains. The ending should fit the facts rather than manufacture a transformation because the course is nearly over.

sections.title: Then spend the time
items: If a remaining saved account, shortcut, or other access to porn matters, remove it without reopening the content.
You don’t need to inspect material first. If there’s nothing relevant left to remove, don’t search for something to delete.
Instead, spend fifteen to twenty minutes on an activity or person you want to keep giving time to.
Use something you’ve already chosen. The course can end with an ordinary part of life, not another elaborate reflection about recovery.

sections.title: When the next step is help
items: If the record suggests a serious ongoing problem, use the support details now. The honest next step may be care beyond this course. A positive closing sentence isn’t more important than that request.

sections.title: What you’ll keep
items: You can finish with a brief note about what you’ll keep and what you’ll give less time to.
Name real actions: putting the phone away, attending the class, keeping an appointment, or stopping repeated searches. Avoid promising that an unfinished difficulty has disappeared.
Keep the useful instructions and reminders after the rest of the material is closed. You don’t need to preserve every page as something to reread whenever you feel uncertain.
Today, review the record and take one fitting action. Another deletion, a complete log, or improvement in every area isn’t required.
What matters is that the action follows what you’ve learned and leaves the next day with something clear to use.

practice: Read an early entry beside a recent one. Note an honest observation, including no clear change where accurate.
Remove remaining access to porn only if relevant and possible without reopening it.
Otherwise spend fifteen to twenty minutes on a person or activity you value. If the record shows a serious continuing problem, use the support details now.
lessons.doneWhen: The record is reviewed and one fitting action is taken. A positive ending or another deletion isn’t required.

lessons.title: Save a short plan for after the course

openingQuote.text: The future is purchased by the present.

closingQuote.text: Dwell on the beauty of life. Watch the stars, and see yourself running with them.

sections.title: The next difficult evening
items: Leave yourself a short plan for the next difficult evening. You should be able to find and read it without opening the whole course.
Make the first action clear. “Close the content and put the phone on the kitchen counter” is easier to follow than “remember my recovery.”
Include an option for times the usual room, device, or activity isn’t available.

sections.title: Reviews and help
items: Save a review in two weeks, and retain the thirty-, sixty-, and ninety-day checks already scheduled.
At each check, ask what’s helping, what’s difficult, and whether more support is needed. Review sooner if control or daily life worsens.

If help is needed now, make the request now. If things are working, use the useful parts and give time to ordinary life. You don’t need to keep studying the problem every evening to take the change seriously.

sections.title: Keep it flexible
items: A missed day doesn’t require restarting. After a slip, end the episode and use the steps you prepared.
After a longer interruption, choose the next reasonable chance to resume. Keep the plan flexible enough for the life you’re actually living.
Save the short version somewhere accessible, with a backup if the device is unavailable. Then begin the next activity you’ve chosen.
You don’t have to promise a future without urges. You have a reason, some practical steps, and a way to ask for more help when you need it.

question.prompt: What needs most attention in the next two weeks?

opts.t: Keep a change that helps
Fix one known gap
Give an activity its next session
Get more suitable support now
Start a clearer observation
Another priority

fb.lead: Give the priority a first action and keep the two-week review.
items: Check activities after they happen. If help is needed now, request it now.

practice: Save a short plan with your goal, early signs, first response, after-slip steps, smaller day, support details, and next review. Keep it accessible, with a backup if needed.
Review the Day 73 block and first Day 77 session if they’ve happened; otherwise keep their reminders.
Set a check in two weeks and retain the thirty-, sixty-, and ninety-day reviews. If control or daily life is worsening, request help now.
lessons.doneWhen: The short plan is saved, due reviews are completed or kept for later, and any needed support request is made.
